NDR ROI Analysis for Enterprise Security Teams: What the 2026 Numbers Actually Show
items.summary: Every security leader eventually gets the same question from the CFO: what do we get back for what we spend on detection tools? For network detection and response, the old answer used to be “fewer bad days.” That doesn’t survive a budget meeting anymore, and honestly, it shouldn’t have for a while. If you’re evaluating NDR , you probably don’t need another explanation of why network visibility matters. You need to know whether a given platform will save enough analyst time, cut enough operational overhead, and provide enough investigation context to justify the spend, and whether that holds up better than a competing architecture would. NDR ROI comes down to what a platform can actually see and how much context it hands an analyst afterward. Flow-only telemetry can tell you two hosts talked to each other; deeper inspection gives an analyst evidence to investigate, hunt with, and act on. That distinction shows up financially in investigation time, analyst workload, how long metadata needs to stick around, and how many separate tools a SOC has to keep running. This piece runs the actual math using 2026 data from IBM, Verizon, Ponemon, and ISC2, works through a sample ROI calculation, and looks at where Fidelis Network ® ‘s architecture changes the return relative to a flow-only approach. The Cost of Not Having Network Visibility Start with what an organization is already paying, whether or not it shows up as a line item. Breach costs keep climbing. The global average cost of a data breach [1] reached $4.99 million in 2026, a 12% increase year over year, driven largely by higher detection, escalation, and lost-business costs tied to AI-enabled attacks. AI-driven breaches specifically rose 56% and now average $6 million each. Speed is still the variable that moves that number most. IBM’s research has put the average breach lifecycle at around 241 days, roughly 181 to identify and 60 to contain, a figure that’s held fairly steady across recent report cycles. Organizations leaning heavily on AI and automated response capabilities in their security operations reduced breach costs by close to $2 million on average compared with organizations using none. Every extra day a threat goes unnoticed adds to that total. Attackers are increasingly exploiting software vulnerabilities and third-party relationships rather than relying solely on stolen credentials. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report [2] , built on more than 22,000 confirmed breaches, found vulnerability exploitation became the leading breach entry point, and third-party or supply-chain involvement jumped 60% year over year to touch 48% of breaches. Both trends reinforce the need for visibility beyond the endpoint: exploited vulnerabilities and abused third-party connections can generate network activity that endpoint-focused controls may not fully contextualize. Insider activity and lateral movement are a hidden line item too. The 2026 Ponemon Institute Cost of Insider Risks study [3] found average annual insider risk cost hit $19.5 million, up from $17.4 million the year before, with credential-theft incidents averaging $842,462 each. Most of these incidents involve someone moving across internal network traffic they don’t normally touch, so containment speed swings the cost hard: incidents contained inside 30 days averaged $14.2 million in annual organizational cost, versus $21.9 million once containment stretched past 90 days. That gap alone is the financial case for watching internal networks, not only the perimeter. Encrypted traffic hides a lot of this too. Nearly all web traffic is encrypted now, and because encrypted traffic dominates enterprise network environments, attackers increasingly hide malicious activity inside SSL/TLS sessions specifically to dodge tools that stop inspecting at the edge of encryption. A detection approach that can’t see inside those sessions is missing a real slice of what’s crossing the wire. Staffing shortages make everything above harder to manage. ISC2’s most recent workforce research [4] found that critical skills gaps, not headcount alone, are now the binding constraint on security operations, and organizations with significant skills gaps are nearly twice as likely to suffer a material breach. Every security leader eventually gets the same question from the CFO: what do we get back for what we spend on detection tools? For network detection and response, the old answer used to be “fewer bad days.” That doesn’t survive a budget meeting anymore, and honestly, it shouldn’t have for a while.

If you’re evaluating NDR, you probably don’t need another explanation of why network visibility matters. You need to know whether a given platform will save enough analyst time, cut enough operational overhead, and provide enough investigation context to justify the spend, and whether that holds up better than a competing architecture would. NDR ROI comes down to what a platform can actually see and how much context it hands an analyst afterward. Flow-only telemetry can tell you two hosts talked to each other; deeper inspection gives an analyst evidence to investigate, hunt with, and act on. That distinction shows up financially in investigation time, analyst workload, how long metadata needs to stick around, and how many separate tools a SOC has to keep running.

This piece runs the actual math using 2026 data from IBM, Verizon, Ponemon, and ISC2, works through a sample ROI calculation, and looks at where Fidelis Network®‘s architecture changes the return relative to a flow-only approach.

The Cost of Not Having Network Visibility

Start with what an organization is already paying, whether or not it shows up as a line item.

Breach costs keep climbing. The global average cost of a data breach[1] reached $4.99 million in 2026, a 12% increase year over year, driven largely by higher detection, escalation, and lost-business costs tied to AI-enabled attacks. AI-driven breaches specifically rose 56% and now average $6 million each.

Speed is still the variable that moves that number most. IBM’s research has put the average breach lifecycle at around 241 days, roughly 181 to identify and 60 to contain, a figure that’s held fairly steady across recent report cycles. Organizations leaning heavily on AI and automated response capabilities in their security operations reduced breach costs by close to $2 million on average compared with organizations using none. Every extra day a threat goes unnoticed adds to that total.

Attackers are increasingly exploiting software vulnerabilities and third-party relationships rather than relying solely on stolen credentials. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report[2], built on more than 22,000 confirmed breaches, found vulnerability exploitation became the leading breach entry point, and third-party or supply-chain involvement jumped 60% year over year to touch 48% of breaches. Both trends reinforce the need for visibility beyond the endpoint: exploited vulnerabilities and abused third-party connections can generate network activity that endpoint-focused controls may not fully contextualize.

Insider activity and lateral movement are a hidden line item too. The 2026 Ponemon Institute Cost of Insider Risks study[3] found average annual insider risk cost hit $19.5 million, up from $17.4 million the year before, with credential-theft incidents averaging $842,462 each. Most of these incidents involve someone moving across internal network traffic they don’t normally touch, so containment speed swings the cost hard: incidents contained inside 30 days averaged $14.2 million in annual organizational cost, versus $21.9 million once containment stretched past 90 days. That gap alone is the financial case for watching internal networks, not only the perimeter.

Encrypted traffic hides a lot of this too. Nearly all web traffic is encrypted now, and because encrypted traffic dominates enterprise network environments, attackers increasingly hide malicious activity inside SSL/TLS sessions specifically to dodge tools that stop inspecting at the edge of encryption. A detection approach that can’t see inside those sessions is missing a real slice of what’s crossing the wire.

Staffing shortages make everything above harder to manage. ISC2’s most recent workforce research[4] found that critical skills gaps, not headcount alone, are now the binding constraint on security operations, and organizations with significant skills gaps are nearly twice as likely to suffer a material breach. Fewer people means every hour a security analyst loses to a false positive is an hour not spent on something real.

Where NDR ROI Comes From

NDR earns its budget in five places. Each one ties back to a cost the organization is already absorbing, even if finance doesn’t track it as an NDR line item.

Faster detection and response

Continuous monitoring of network traffic, paired with machine learning and behavioral analytics that model normal network behavior, lets a platform identify anomalies and flag network events without waiting on a matching signature. Shrink the identify-and-contain window and you lower the average cost of every incident, since faster resolution correlates with lower total costs across both IBM’s and Ponemon’s research.

Real-Time Insight, Real-Time Prevention with Fidelis Network
  • Block attacks before damage occurs
  • Prevent lateral movement inside your network
  • Reduce false positives & alert fatigue
Read the Whitepaper
Fewer false positives, less wasted analyst time

Microsoft and Omdia’s State of the SOC 2026 research found that 46% of all security alerts turn out to be false positives, and the 2025 SANS Detection and Response Survey[5] found 73% of security teams name false positives their single biggest detection challenge. Correlating related alerts into one validated incident cuts that noise at the source.

Visibility endpoint tools structurally cannot provide

Endpoint detection only sees managed devices, with no line of sight into unmanaged devices, IoT, or OT gear. Network traffic analysis, working from raw network packets rather than agent data, can provide visibility into those unmanaged devices and environments that may not support an agent at all, which is exactly the blind spot SANS’s 2025 survey flagged in organizations leaning too heavily on endpoint-only detection.

Insider threat and lateral movement detection

Once someone is inside, the next moves are internal network traffic: scanning, credential reuse, unusual remote access, control communications trying to phone home, sometimes stretched out over months in the pattern typical of advanced persistent threats. Organizations that contained insider incidents within 30 days reported roughly $7.7 million less in annual organizational cost than those taking more than 90 days, which makes catching lateral movement early one of the more directly quantifiable ROI levers a security team has.

Encrypted traffic and hidden threats

With most web traffic now encrypted, sophisticated attacks increasingly hide inside encrypted network traffic to evade tools that stop inspecting at the edge of TLS. Deep packet inspection and metadata-based analysis catch what’s exposing sensitive data inside those sessions without needing plaintext content every time.

These five drivers don’t come free with every architecture. Some NDR solutions rely mostly on flow telemetry, lighter to run but thinner for an analyst mid-investigation. Others add deeper packet inspection and full content analysis, hold richer metadata longer, and pair detection with correlated, evidence-backed alerts instead of a raw feed. That difference shows up directly in investigation time and in how much of the ROI modeled on paper survives contact with production traffic.

Example: What the Savings Look Like

Numbers land better than formulas do. Here’s a simplified calculation an enterprise security team can rebuild with its own inputs; the figures are illustrative, not a published benchmark, since actual results shift with traffic profile and tuning.

Assume a mid-size SOC running eight analysts, fielding 1,200 network-related alerts a week, with roughly 46% turning out to be false positives, matching the industry figure cited above. This example assumes correlation and behavioral analysis bring that rate down to somewhere near 25%. The post-NDR values below are scenario assumptions built to illustrate the model, not Fidelis performance benchmarks or figures from any published study.

MetricBefore NDRScenario after NDRNotes Weekly network alerts1,200~700 correlatedCorrelation cuts what an analyst has to individually reviewFalse-positive rate46%~25% (Note: It's just an example)Behavioral correlation and session context reduce mistriageAnalyst hours on triage/week320210Scenario assumption based on modeled analyst workload, not derived from the alert counts above; replace with your team's measured triage timeHours freed up/week-110Redirected to investigation and proactive threat huntingLoaded analyst hourly cost$85$85Sample blended rate; swap in your ownWeekly labor value freed-$9,350110 hours x $85Annualized labor value-~$486,00052 weeks, before PTO or holiday adjustments

The point isn’t that every organization will free exactly 110 analyst hours a week. The point is that NDR ROI can be modeled using three numbers you already have: alert volume, false-positive rate, and loaded analyst cost. Replace the assumptions above with your own, then weigh the resulting labor value against each vendor’s license and operating costs before you take anything to finance. That’s the comparison that actually decides a procurement decision, not a vendor’s headline detection claim.

Deployment Economics: What it Costs to Run

ROI isn’t only about the license. It’s about what it takes to keep the platform running month after month, and that’s usually where a business case quietly falls apart six months in.

Is it delivered as an on-premises appliance, a virtual machine, a cloud subscription, or some blend of the three? Sensor-based deployments typically place hardware or virtual sensors at ingress and egress points and at key internal segments, then centralize analysis and storage elsewhere. Cost has at least three moving parts because of that: sensor count and placement, how long metadata gets retained, and the compute needed to run detection at line rate across your network infrastructure.

Storage duration matters more than most buyers assume going in. Retrospective analysis, going back through historical metadata once new threat intelligence surfaces, only works if that metadata is still around. Retention windows that are too short quietly erase the value of retrospective detection before it ever pays off.

Maintenance and patching are the recurring cost most ROI models leave out entirely. On-premises deployment means your team owns updates, tuning, and uptime, indefinitely, on top of everything else on the calendar. A cloud-delivered model shifts that operational load onto the vendor, which changes the labor side of the equation even when the license line looks similar on paper. Watch pricing structure closely, too: some cloud NDR pricing scales with the number of sensors deployed, which can work against an organization that’s expanding coverage. Pricing tied to protected bandwidth and retention days instead may be easier to forecast as the network grows, since it tracks what’s actually being protected rather than how many boxes had to go up to protect it.

How Fidelis Network® Changes the ROI Equation

Here’s what that architecture difference looks like in an actual product, organized around the financial questions a buyer actually needs answered rather than a feature list.

How much investigation work is still left for the analyst?

Fidelis Network® uses patented Deep Session Inspection to provide deep visibility into complete network communications and inspect embedded, compressed, and obfuscated content, across all ports and protocols, rather than sampling flow records. It also supports packet capture and real-time Layer 7 analysis and collects over 300 metadata attributes well beyond typical flow-based telemetry. That’s more investigation context available in the same platform, which can reduce the amount of manual reconstruction an analyst has to do before an investigation even starts, rather than a guaranteed reduction in hours.

How much of that context arrives already correlated?

Fidelis Network® is built around aggregated alerts, context, and evidence rather than a raw alert feed. The platform automatically validates, correlates, and consolidates related network alerts into a single view instead of leaving an analyst to piece together suspicious activity from a dozen separate notifications. This is the mechanism the worked example above is pricing in. NDR ROI isn’t determined by detection alone; it’s determined by how much analyst work happens after detection, and aggregated, evidence-backed alerts are the lever that cuts that work down.

How many separate tools do you need to operate?

Fidelis Network® bundles sandboxing, DLP, threat intelligence, and network forensics into one platform with alerts mapped against the MITRE ATT&CK framework, instead of requiring separate point tools for each capability. Consolidating those capabilities into one platform can reduce the number of separate tools, consoles, and integrations a team has to operate day to day, though the actual reduction depends on what a given team already runs.

How do you handle encrypted web traffic?

The Fidelis Web Sensor integrates over ICAP and S-ICAP with proxies and network devices that already decrypt traffic for other purposes, and can redirect policy-violating sessions to an informative page instead of dropping them outright. Because the Web Sensor can receive that decrypted content directly from a compatible proxy, organizations can inspect proxied encrypted web traffic without deploying a separate decryption server just for the Web Sensor.

Who owns the infrastructure as the network grows?

Fidelis Network® Cloud prices on two variables: aggregate peak protected bandwidth and days of metadata retention, which organizations with rapidly expanding environments may find easier to forecast than per-sensor pricing. Fidelis manages the hosted infrastructure itself, including software updates, patches, monitoring, and support, while the customer retains responsibility for positioning sensors, managing alerts, and maintaining custom policies. That’s less infrastructure to operate, not zero operational responsibility.

Each point above answers a question raised earlier: where the investigation-time savings come from, why the labor math in the worked example holds up, and why the deployment-cost side can be easier to forecast as the network scales.

Fitting into the Stack You Already Have

A platform doesn’t operate in isolation, though. NDR ROI depends heavily on how cleanly a platform integrates with the security information and event management (SIEM) and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) tools already running in a security operations center, plus the EDR handling the endpoint side of things. A platform that leans on manual response capabilities for every action, instead of feeding automated response into an existing playbook, adds staffing overhead that eats into the labor savings modeled above. Seamless integration with what a team already owns is often a bigger factor in improving security posture than any single detection feature, because it decides whether alerts turn into faster response or just pile up in yet another queue nobody has time to watch.

A Checklist Before You Buy

This is the part worth taking into a vendor evaluation directly. Enabling security teams to actually use what a platform detects, not just adding another feed of potential security threats, is the real test. Whatever platform you’re comparing, get direct answers to these before finalizing an ROI model:

  • Does it decode and inspect full content at wire speed, or mostly flow records and sampled metadata?
  • Does it hand analysts aggregated alerts with context and evidence, or a raw stream they have to correlate manually?
  • Can it consume decrypted traffic from your existing proxies without forcing a second TLS termination point?
  • Does it integrate with your existing SIEM, SOAR, and EDR, and offer threat intelligence integration, so alerts feed one incident response workflow instead of another disconnected console?
  • Does pricing scale with what you're protecting (bandwidth, retention) or with how you happen to be segmented (sensor count, appliance count)?
  • Who owns patching, uptime, and infrastructure maintenance, and what does that cost your team in hours if the answer is "you do"?
  • How much does its alert correlation actually reduce the false-positive rate your analysts deal with day to day, not just how many capabilities sit on the datasheet?

Run these against any platform, including Fidelis Network®, and score the answers against the labor-value model from the worked example above. That comparison, not a feature list, is what should decide the purchase.

The Bottom Line

NDR ROI comes down to what happens after detection as much as detection itself. A platform that surfaces aggregated alerts with context and evidence, rather than raw signals an analyst has to piece together, is the difference between a labor-savings model that holds up in production and one that only worked on a slide deck.

Build your NDR business case with your own alert volume, analyst costs, protected bandwidth, and retention requirements. See how Fidelis Network® maps those inputs to a deployment and ROI model for your environment.

Frequently Asked Questions
How is NDR different from a firewall or IPS for ROI purposes?

Firewalls and IPS make allow-or-block decisions mostly at the perimeter and lean on known threat signatures. NDR catches anomalies in normal network behavior after traffic is already inside, exactly where lateral movement, insider activity, and post-compromise behavior happen. The ROI comes from catching what perimeter tools structurally can’t see.

Can NDR replace endpoint detection and response instead of adding to the budget?

No, and treating it that way undersells both. EDR sees managed-device activity; NDR sees everything crossing the network, including unmanaged devices and IoT. The stronger case treats them as complementary layers feeding one response workflow, not competing line items on the same budget.

How long does it typically take to see ROI from an NDR deployment?

Labor-efficiency ROI can be measured once a deployment has established a reliable baseline for alert volume, false-positive rates, and analyst triage time, so track those three from day one rather than waiting to evaluate the platform. Breach-cost-avoidance ROI takes longer to demonstrate, since it depends on incidents that don’t happen, which is exactly why a labor-savings model like the one above is worth building up front rather than after the fact.

Does NDR ROI hold up for organizations that already inspect TLS at the proxy or firewall?

Yes, often more so. If a compatible web proxy already decrypts traffic, Fidelis Web Sensor can receive that decrypted content over ICAP/S-ICAP for inspection, which gets full content visibility without adding a second decryption point, usually cheaper than layering separate TLS inspection into every new tool added afterward.

What's a reasonable false-positive reduction target to build into an ROI model?

There isn’t a universal target. Industry benchmarks put the baseline false-positive rate near 46%, but the right reduction to model depends on your current tooling, tuning maturity, and traffic profile. Use your own current rate as the baseline, then model one or more improvement scenarios, the way the worked example above uses a 25% scenario, rather than assuming a fixed post-NDR number as an industry standard.

items.title: Critical VMware vCenter Flaws Let Hackers Bypass Authentication and Access Servers
items.summary: Broadcom has released fixes for five VMware flaws, and one lets anyone with network access to vCenter skip login. Broadcom published the advisory, VMSA-2026-0009 , on November 19, 2026. It covers vCenter, SDDC Manager, and VMware Tools. CVSS scores range from 6.7 to 9.8, and Broadcom has listed no workarounds. The most critical flaw is CVE-2026-123890 , an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service. It has a CVSS score of 9.8. VMware vCenter Vulnerabilities A remote user with network access to vCenter can get in without valid credentials and take control of the system. The score reflects that no login, no user action, and no special access is needed. Mandiant reported the issue to Broadcom. vCenter is the main console for managing virtual machines, hosts, storage, and networks, so it holds a lot of power in one place. Anyone who controls it can change settings, create accounts, and reach the data stored on virtual disks. Readers may remember a similar bug from July. Cyber Security News covered the earlier VMSA-2026-0006 flaws , including CVE-2026-59309, another directory service bypass. Within days, hackers scanned for exposed vCenter servers, as seen in a report on hackers scanning for vCenter systems . A later report described a web shell campaign that used a different vCenter bug, CVE-2026-59310. That campaign ended with ransomware on ESXi hosts. I found no report of active use for the new flaw yet, but this history shows how fast attackers move after a disclosure. One analysis says this is a new bug and not a repeat of the July one, even though both sit in the same service. It also says ESX is not affected by this advisory. Three SDDC Manager Flaws SDDC Manager, the tool used in VMware Cloud Foundation, has three flaws. CVE-2026-123891 is an SQL injection with a score of 8.1. A logged-in user can send a crafted query to read or write database records. CVE-2026-123892 is a command injection with a score of 7.2. It lets a logged-in user run commands on the appliance. CVE-2026-123893 is a local privilege escalation with a score of 6.7. An admin on SDDC Manager can escalate to root. Arnoldas Radisauskas of NATO NCSC reported all three. The patches are cumulative, so version 9.1.1.0200 carries every fix, as noted in the SDDC Manager 9.1.1.0200 release notes . CVE-2026-123894 affects VMware Tools for Windows and has a score of 6.7. It is a SAML token signature bypass. A user with a local privileged process on a Windows guest that uses Guest Alias mapping can raise their privileges inside that VM. Noam Pomerantz reported it. This is not the first VMware Tools problem of its kind. An earlier VMware Tools authentication bypass was fixed in 2025. Admins who patched that one will need to update again. For vCenter, the fixed builds are 9.1.1.0200 , 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m . Cloud Foundation 5.x users should apply 5.2.5. Telco Cloud users should follow KB463116 . vCenter 7.0 has no public fix, so customers with extended support must contact Broadcom. For SDDC Manager, use 9.1.1.0200 or 9.0.2.0100. For VMware Tools, update to 13.1.5.0 or 12.5.5. Product Component Affected version CVE(s) Patched version VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.1.x.x CVE-2026-123890 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.0.x.x CVE-2026-123890 9.0.2.0200 VMware vCenter vCenter 8.0 CVE-2026-123890 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter vCenter 7.0 CVE-2026-123890 No public fix. Contact Broadcom Support if you have an extended support contract VMware Cloud Foundation vCenter 5.x CVE-2026-123890 5.2.5 (see KB88287) VMware Telco Cloud Platform vCenter 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2 CVE-2026-123890 See KB463116 VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure vCenter 3.0 CVE-2026-123890 See KB463116 VMware Cloud Foundation SDDC Manager 9.1.x.x CVE-2026-123891, CVE-2026-123892 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation SDDC Manager / VCF Installer 9.1.x.x CVE-2026-123893 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation SDDC Manager 9.0.x.x CVE-2026-123891, CVE-2026-123892 9.0.2.0100 VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation SDDC Manager / VCF Installer 9.0.x.x CVE-2026-123893 9.0.2.0100 VMware Cloud Foundation SDDC Manager 5.x CVE-2026-123891, CVE-2026-123892, CVE-2026-123893 5.2.5 VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation VMware Tools (Windows) 13.x.x.x CVE-2026-123894 13.1.5.0 VMware Tools VMware Tools (Windows) 13.x.x.x CVE-2026-123894 13.1.5.0 VMware Tools VMware Tools (Windows) 12.3.x CVE-2026-123894 12.5.5 (12.4.10, which is part of 12.5.5, also fixes Windows 32-bit) Because no workaround exists, patching is the only real fix. Teams should find every vCenter system, check whether any can be reached from untrusted networks, and limit access to approved admin networks. They should also review logs for new accounts, permission changes, and odd login events. Broadcom’s FAQ for this advisory gives more detail. SDDC Manager, the tool used in VMware Cloud Foundation, has three flaws. CVE-2026-123891 is an SQL injection with a score of 8.1. A logged-in user can send a crafted query to read or write database records.

CVE-2026-123892 is a command injection with a score of 7.2. It lets a logged-in user run commands on the appliance. CVE-2026-123893 is a local privilege escalation with a score of 6.7. An admin on SDDC Manager can escalate to root.

Arnoldas Radisauskas of NATO NCSC reported all three. The patches are cumulative, so version 9.1.1.0200 carries every fix, as noted in the SDDC Manager 9.1.1.0200 release notes.

CVE-2026-123894 affects VMware Tools for Windows and has a score of 6.7. It is a SAML token signature bypass. A user with a local privileged process on a Windows guest that uses Guest Alias mapping can raise their privileges inside that VM. Noam Pomerantz reported it.

This is not the first VMware Tools problem of its kind. An earlier VMware Tools authentication bypass was fixed in 2025. Admins who patched that one will need to update again.

For vCenter, the fixed builds are 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m. Cloud Foundation 5.x users should apply 5.2.5. Telco Cloud users should follow KB463116.

vCenter 7.0 has no public fix, so customers with extended support must contact Broadcom. For SDDC Manager, use 9.1.1.0200 or 9.0.2.0100. For VMware Tools, update to 13.1.5.0 or 12.5.5.

They should also review logs for new accounts, permission changes, and odd login events. Broadcom’s FAQ for this advisory gives more detail.

items.title: JPMorgan Chase Confirms Third-Party Cyberattack That May Have Exposed Customer Names and Emails
items.summary: JPMorgan Chase confirmed on November 19 that a cyberattack targeted outside companies that provide services to the bank. The bank said it believes attackers accessed marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses. It did not say how many customers may be affected. J.P. Morgan and Chase said in statements on X that the attack did not disrupt banking services. The bank plans to contact affected customers directly where appropriate and offer support, including free credit monitoring. We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack. Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.… — J.P. Morgan (@jpmorgan) November 19, 2026 It did not say when those notices would go out or how long the monitoring would last. JPMorgan Chase Confirms Third-Party Data Breach The bank has not named the vendors, said how attackers gained access, or confirmed whether they copied the records. Its statement did not identify passwords, card numbers, or transaction records among the data believed to have been accessed. It also did not provide a full list of the information stored in the affected records. We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack. Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.… — Chase (@Chase) November 19, 2026 The disclosure points to data held outside the bank, not a confirmed break-in at JPMorgan Chase itself. The separate SitusAMC data breach showed how an attack on a financial services vendor could expose client records while the vendor’s services stayed online. In this case, JPMorgan Chase has described the exposed material as marketing data. Reuters reported that a JPMorgan spokesperson ruled out a connection between the cyberattack and the service disruption some customers experienced earlier in the week. Chase had attributed that earlier incident to a software bug in systems running on its own hardware and said it had found no evidence of a cyberattack behind the outage. Names and email addresses can help scammers make fake breach notices look real. A message might address a customer by name and ask them to sign in to claim free credit monitoring. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate phishing campaign that copied Chase login pages . No public evidence links that campaign to this incident. Customers who receive an unexpected notice should avoid clicking its links or opening attachments. They can verify the message by calling the number on the back of their card. Chase’s fraud reporting page says customers can forward suspicious emails to phishing@chase.com and should contact the bank right away if they spot an unauthorized charge or believe their account was compromised. The key questions for customers are which records the attackers reached and who will receive a notice. For security teams, the unanswered question is how the attackers got in. Until JPMorgan Chase releases more details, the disclosure confirms an attack on service providers, but it does not establish the full scope of the customer data exposure. Chase said the third-party cyberattack was unrelated to the November 16 Chase outage . The bank traced that disruption to a temporary software bug on its own systems and said it found no evidence of a cyberattack What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. items.title: The FBI ARTEX Advisory and the Paths to Your Critical Systems
items.summary: The FBI’s November 13 FLASH advisory on ARTEX describes attackers using an agentic penetration testing framework to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, privilege escalation, and other stages of an intrusion. Some attacks progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. That speed creates an urgent problem for defenders. It also makes an existing question harder to postpone: if an attacker compromises an identity in your environment, what can that identity reach? The answer depends on more than the privileges assigned directly to that account. Group memberships, application ownership, delegation, deployment permissions, and cross-platform trust can combine to provide access that no individual permission review makes obvious. Those connections determine how an initial foothold can become control over a critical system. The FBI’s ARTEX advisory gives organizations a concrete reason to examine those connections now. The techniques described in the advisory span on-premises and cloud environments. They include enumerating identity permissions, abusing application access, and escalating privileges. An attacker can use each discovery to choose the next action. A credential provides access to an application. The application’s permissions provide control over another identity. That identity holds authority over a more sensitive resource. Microsoft’s analysis of ARTEX activity describes agents accumulating discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph as they work. ARTEX uses those connections to choose its next move. Defenders can build that view before an intrusion, identify the permissions that expose critical systems, and remove them before an attacker takes advantage. For more on reducing this exposure, see our report, AI Security Starts With Eliminating Attack Paths . ConnectWise illustrates the consequence of trusted access The ConnectWise campaign is a useful example. Microsoft reported attackers using compromised application credentials to authenticate to customer environments through access those applications had already been granted. The application’s permissions became the attacker’s permissions. Follow-on activity included reconnaissance and changes to credentials and privileges that could support expanded or persistent access. This is why reviewing a vendor application requires more than confirming that the vendor is legitimate. Security teams need to understand the application’s effective authority: What resources can it access or control? Can it grant additional privileges or affect other identities? Who can change its credentials, ownership, or permissions? What critical systems are reachable through those relationships? These questions apply to backup products, deployment identities, business integrations, and other trusted applications. They are also the questions organizations should be able to answer before a vendor reports a compromise. Get the ConnectWise tenant review guide to learn how to use BloodHound to examine the applications’ access and paths to critical assets. Turning the FBI’s ARTEX recommendations into action The FBI’s recommendations cover a broad defensive program. BloodHound Enterprise helps address the identity and access relationships within that program by showing how permissions connect to critical assets and where remediation can break an attack path. Four areas deserve attention. Application permissions and privileged identities. Review service principals, application ownership, role assignments, and consent grants in the context of what they enable. An application can create significant exposure through its own privileges or through its ability to control another identity. BHE identifies attack paths involving these relationships , including paths from third-party applications with privileged access to the customer’s tenant. Deployment and CI/CD authority. The advisory explicitly addresses deployment credentials, publishing interfaces, infrastructure-as-code, and CI/CD pipelines. These systems deserve scrutiny because permission to influence a build or deployment can carry authority over downstream infrastructure. BHE connects GitHub repository and workflow permissions with AWS and Azure permissions and trust relationships, helping teams identify where control over a pipeline creates a path into production. Certificate services and administrative boundaries. Review AD CS weaknesses and the relationships that allow identities to cross into more privileged systems. Privilege Zones let organizations focus attack path analysis on selected critical assets, including business systems that require protection beyond traditional Tier Zero / Control Plane infrastructure. Remediation priorities. Finding excessive access creates a queue of work. Understanding how that access contributes to attack paths helps teams decide what to fix first. The effective change may sit several steps upstream from the asset at risk: a GitHub permission, an application owner, a group membership, or a cloud trust relationship. Reduce exposure before an intrusion The FBI notes that ARTEX can generate noisy activity and trigger alerts, yet move fast enough to leave little time for a coordinated response. An alert starts a process: someone still has to investigate, establish the scope, and contain the attacker’s access. When privileged access is possible in under three hours, the permissions already in place can have consequences before that process is complete. A path removed beforehand gives the attacker one fewer opportunity and defenders one fewer route to contain. After a decade of simulating advanced adversaries, we know the value of an attacker getting in and finding nowhere to go. Making that outcome more likely requires a practical way to reduce exposure at scale. The average BloodHound Enterprise customer starts with over 1 billion attack paths. Addressing them individually is not workable. BHE prioritizes choke

The ConnectWise campaign is a useful example. Microsoft reported attackers using compromised application credentials to authenticate to customer environments through access those applications had already been granted. 

The application’s permissions became the attacker’s permissions. Follow-on activity included reconnaissance and changes to credentials and privileges that could support expanded or persistent access. 

This is why reviewing a vendor application requires more than confirming that the vendor is legitimate. Security teams need to understand the application’s effective authority: 

  • What resources can it access or control? 
  • Can it grant additional privileges or affect other identities? 
  • Who can change its credentials, ownership, or permissions? 
  • What critical systems are reachable through those relationships? 

These questions apply to backup products, deployment identities, business integrations, and other trusted applications. They are also the questions organizations should be able to answer before a vendor reports a compromise.

Turning the FBI’s ARTEX recommendations into action 

The FBI’s recommendations cover a broad defensive program. BloodHound Enterprise helps address the identity and access relationships within that program by showing how permissions connect to critical assets and where remediation can break an attack path. 

Four areas deserve attention. 

Application permissions and privileged identities. Review service principals, application ownership, role assignments, and consent grants in the context of what they enable. An application can create significant exposure through its own privileges or through its ability to control another identity. BHE identifies attack paths involving these relationships, including paths from third-party applications with privileged access to the customer’s tenant. 

Deployment and CI/CD authority. The advisory explicitly addresses deployment credentials, publishing interfaces, infrastructure-as-code, and CI/CD pipelines. These systems deserve scrutiny because permission to influence a build or deployment can carry authority over downstream infrastructure. BHE connects GitHub repository and workflow permissions with AWS and Azure permissions and trust relationships, helping teams identify where control over a pipeline creates a path into production. 

Certificate services and administrative boundaries. Review AD CS weaknesses and the relationships that allow identities to cross into more privileged systems. Privilege Zones let organizations focus attack path analysis on selected critical assets, including business systems that require protection beyond traditional Tier Zero / Control Plane infrastructure. 

Remediation priorities. Finding excessive access creates a queue of work. Understanding how that access contributes to attack paths helps teams decide what to fix first. The effective change may sit several steps upstream from the asset at risk: a GitHub permission, an application owner, a group membership, or a cloud trust relationship. 

Reduce exposure before an intrusion 

The FBI notes that ARTEX can generate noisy activity and trigger alerts, yet move fast enough to leave little time for a coordinated response. An alert starts a process: someone still has to investigate, establish the scope, and contain the attacker’s access. When privileged access is possible in under three hours, the permissions already in place can have consequences before that process is complete. 

A path removed beforehand gives the attacker one fewer opportunity and defenders one fewer route to contain. After a decade of simulating advanced adversaries, we know the value of an attacker getting in and finding nowhere to go. Making that outcome more likely requires a practical way to reduce exposure at scale. 

The average BloodHound Enterprise customer starts with over 1 billion attack paths. Addressing them individually is not workable. BHE prioritizes choke points: relationships shared by many paths, where a single remediation can eliminate thousands of individual attack paths at once. That lets teams make meaningful progress without treating every route as a separate task. 

On average, BloodHound Enterprise customers reduce their attack path exposure by 40% within the first 30 days. Teams can also track the resulting reduction in exposure to critical assets and report that progress to the board. Ongoing analysis helps them identify when changes to identities, permissions, or trust relationships introduce new paths, so the work continues as the environment changes. 

Where to start 

Organizations responding to the FBI’s ARTEX advisory can begin with a focused set of questions: 

  • Which third-party applications can reach critical resources or gain higher privileges? 
  • Who can control those applications and their credentials? 
  • Who can influence deployment workflows, and what production authority do those workflows hold? 
  • Which identities have unintended paths into Tier Zero / Control Plane or other sensitive systems? 
  • Which permission changes would remove the most exposure? 

Choose a critical system and work backward through the identities, permissions, and trust relationships that can reach it. Use that analysis to prioritize fixes, then check that those fixes removed the intended paths. 

Our team can help customers conduct that focused review with BloodHound Enterprise. The objective is to reduce what an attacker can accomplish with the access they obtain.

items.title: Criminal IP Launches AITEM to Connect Asset Discovery with AI-Powered Exposure Management
items.summary: Torrance, California, USA, November 19th, 2026, CyberNewswire Criminal IP , a cyber threat intelligence platform developed by AI SPERA, officially launched Criminal IP AITEM (AI-Powered Threat Exposure Management) on November 18, 2026. An evolution of Criminal IP ASM, AITEM combines internet-facing asset discovery with AI-assisted investigation, public-source exposure analysis, and dark web monitoring. It also introduces AI Pentest to help security teams assess and validate security risks in their web assets. Discovering an unfamiliar server or a leaked credential is the first step. Analysts still need to establish how it relates to their organization, assess the surrounding threat signals, and decide whether it requires immediate attention. Criminal IP AITEM brings these findings and their context together so teams can understand what is exposed and decide where to act. A Broader View of Organizational Exposure Forgotten servers, publicly accessible configuration files, and compromised credentials can be difficult to assess when findings are scattered across separate tools. Criminal IP AITEM brings these exposures into a single view so teams can investigate them in the context of their environment. Criminal IP AITEM dashboard summarizes asset inventory, risk distribution, recent findings, and exposure trends The dashboard gives teams an overview of discovered assets and detected risks. Analysts can drill down into individual assets to investigate specific findings and explore related infrastructure. Criminal IP AITEM continuously discovers internet-facing assets and collects information such as IP addresses, domains, certificates, open ports, cloud assets, and technologies. Analysts can use these details to understand how an unfamiliar system connects to their organization. Exposure Beyond Managed Infrastructure Criminal IP AITEM identifies publicly accessible information through search engine analysis and GitHub exposure detection Public-source exposure analysis helps teams find sensitive files, administrative pages, and exposed directories indexed by search engines. GitHub exposure detection helps uncover publicly accessible credentials, API keys, and configuration files associated with the organization. Dark web monitoring surfaces leaked credentials, exposed information, and mentions of the organization across monitored sources. Available source details help analysts assess each finding and decide what to investigate next. AI Across the Exposure Lifecycle AI-Powered at Every Step: Detect, Investigate, Prioritize, and Automate Criminal IP AITEM applies AI across detection, investigation, prioritization, and automation. It connects emerging vulnerabilities with potentially affected assets and supports natural-language queries across assets, vulnerabilities, and exposures, reducing the need for complex filters and repeated manual searches. Prioritization considers exposure severity, asset impact, and threat context to help teams decide which findings need attention first. Automated alerts and investigation workflows support follow-up and reduce manual tracking as risks change. For example, when Criminal IP AITEM discovers an unfamiliar server, analysts can review its open ports, exposed services, SSL/TLS configurations, and related CVEs. Criminal IP threat intelligence adds context through connected infrastructure, malicious activity, abuse history, and associated threat indicators. Together, these details help analysts assess the server’s potential impact and decide what to investigate first. Validating Web Asset Risks with AI Pentest Criminal IP AITEM’s AI Pentest capability enables security teams to run AI-powered penetration tests on their web assets. Teams can use it to identify potential vulnerabilities and validate suspected security weaknesses, giving them additional evidence to decide which findings require remediation. Continuous Monitoring as Exposure Changes As organizations deploy services and work with external suppliers, their exposure changes. Criminal IP AITEM uses daily scans, historical tracking, and automated notifications to help teams follow those changes. Monitoring can also extend to partners and suppliers. With Criminal IP AITEM, Criminal IP connects asset visibility with exposure investigation and ongoing monitoring. Security teams can better understand what is exposed, why a finding matters, and where to focus their next action. Learn more about Criminal IP AITEM. About Criminal IP Criminal IP is AI SPERA’s flagship cyber threat intelligence platform. Used in more than 150 countries, it provides comprehensive threat visibility through Criminal IP Search, Criminal IP ASM, Criminal IP FDS, and Criminal IP TI Feed. Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake. Contact Michael Sena AI SPERA support@aispera.com

items.title: PHP Warns of Critical Security Flaws Affecting All Supported Versions, Urges Users to Update
items.summary: The PHP security team has warned of vulnerabilities across all branches covered by its November 19, 2026 security update, with the most severe issues rated critical. The team urged website operators and hosting providers to update promptly. The critical flaws require non-default settings or uncommon setups, so not every installation faces the same risk. The November security releases are PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36. These are updates for existing PHP branches, so administrators can patch without moving applications to a new branch. The advance notice set a release window of 14:00 to 14:30 UTC and said the updates were part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle. As Cyber Security News noted in its earlier coverage of the PHP warning , the release window fell on the planned launch date for PHP 8.6.0. The two events serve different purposes. Teams that need to close security gaps can patch the branch they already run without rushing a move to PHP 8.6. PHP Security Update Covers One issue PHP flagged before the November release is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw tied to session upload progress. The feature lets an application track a file upload while it is still underway. The team urged website operators and hosting providers to update promptly. The critical flaws require non-default settings or uncommon setups, so not every installation faces the same risk.

items.title: Authenticate Update 43130: Introducing the Atom Viewer, the new Adobe RAW Conversion Watermark filter in the Global category, and much more!
items.summary: Reading time: 11 min What can a video’s structure reveal about its history? How can forensic analysts better detect traces of image manipulation? Authenticate’s latest update brings new tools and practical improvements to help you uncover details that might otherwise go unnoticed during image and video authentication. Let’s explore what’s new! Dear friends, it’s that time again! We’re here with another shining update to Amped Authenticate , your solution for image and video authenticity and integrity analysis! There’s a lot to say: We introduce a new Atom Viewer tab in the Advanced File Info tool for improved integrity analysis; We have a new filter in the Global category to detect the Adobe RAW conversion watermark globally; We improved forgery localization based on the Adobe RAW Watermark by supporting cropping and rotations; We added the ability to draw curves in Annotate; … and many more improvements! Let’s dive into the details! See the New Features in Action Key Takeaways New Atom Viewer for video integrity analysis : Examine the internal structure of MP4 and MOV files to identify differences that may reveal processing or modifications not evident from metadata alone. Global Adobe RAW conversion watermark detection : The new Raw Conversion Watermark filter helps determine whether an image contains the characteristic pattern introduced by Adobe RAW conversion, using a statistical, non-AI-based approach. Improved forgery localization : The Raw Conversion Watermark Map filter now supports images that have undergone cropping or rotations, helping you investigate regions where the watermark may be missing. More flexible annotations and PRNU workflows : Create curved arrows using Bézier curves in Annotate and add notes to Camera Reference Pattern (CRP) log files. AI-free version of Amped Authenticate : You can choose between the standard AI-enabled version and a version without AI-based tools, according to your operational requirements. Additional workflow and reporting improvements : Benefit from clearer metadata source labels, improved bookmark management, more Smart Report output formats, and additional usability enhancements. Introducing the Atom Viewer Why Container Analysis Matters Integrity verification, that is, the process of substantiating whether a file is complete and unaltered since its creation, is an essential part of image authentication. Since we’re talking about the image file history rather than its visual content, this part of the workflow is usually better explored by examining the file properties and structure. Up until now, you could explore the container structure for AVI files with the RIFF Viewer. With this update, we’re covering the MP4-like formats (which include .MOV files) with the new Atom viewer, also found in the Advanced File Info tool. The MP4 Container Format is structured with individual Atoms that contain the data. The way these atoms are organized can be used to compare two files that are supposed to have identical provenance and processing history. The Atom Viewer at Work Let’s work with an example: a Google Pixel 9a smartphone was used to capture a video. Then, the video was trimmed by using the native “Modify” tool to remove several seconds, and saved to the device. Loading the two videos in Authenticate Video Mode and comparing their EXIF data naively, may not be enough to understand that something happened to one of them. For example, the Modify Date was not updated by the Google software. They both show the same date in the original (left) and processed (right) versions. However, if we turn to the Atom Viewer, we immediately notice that the structure is different! In the original video, the MovieBox is located at the bottom, as typically expected for freshly recorded files (since the device doesn’t know when the recording will end, it leaves the MovieBox at the bottom). Instead, for the trimmed file, it has been moved above. If you then open the MovieBox node, you also see that the original file has three tracks, while the processed one misses one of them. You could go on deepening your analysis, and you’d find that the video and audio tracks have also been swapped, that a metadata track that was present in the original file is not retained in the trimmed one, and so on. This was just a quick example to show that even a simple trim on the original recording device leaves substantial traces at the container level. The Atom Viewer is an excellent way to spot them and draw your attention. The Raw Conversion Watermark and Raw Conversion Watermark Map filters You may remember that, with the previous Authenticate update, we introduced the Raw Conversion Watermark filter . Its purpose is to localize forgeries in images by leveraging the presence of the “implicit” watermark left by Adobe Photoshop or Lightroom when converting a RAW image to 8 bit, regardless of the final format. With this release, we’re bringing more power to this feature! First, we’ve renamed the existing filter to Raw Conversion Watermark Map , to better reflect the fact that it produces a forgery localization map by searching for the watermark locally. And more importantly, we’ve added a new filter called Raw Conversion Watermark to the Global category. This one searches for the presence of the watermark in the image as a whole. Let’s see each addition in detail. The new Raw Conversion Watermark filter This filter looks for the presence of the Adobe pattern and returns the obtained statistic, which can be thresholded to get a Yes/No answer. This detection follows the mathematical formulation provided in a recent scientific paper ( J. Butora and P. Bas, “Detection of the Adobe Pattern,” 2024 32nd European Signal Processing Conference (EUSIPCO), Lyon, France, 2024 ) and is not based on AI . When you run the filter on an image, it will check for the presence of the watermark and output a numerical value, which is called “test statistic”. You have to compare this number to a threshold value to determine whether the watermark has been detected sufficiently strongly to claim its presence. To set this value, we ran an experimental validation. For the negative class (images without the watermark), we used a mix of images from the VISION and FLOREVIEW datasets, representing more than 60 different devices that surely do not add the Adobe watermark. We also included several images obtained with DSLR cameras without any Adobe processing. For the positive class (images containing the watermark), we considered a number of images captured with several DSLR camera brands. These images were developed with different versions of Lightroom on multiple devices, and later compressed at various JPEG quality levels. As you can see, the watermark strength varies significantly in the Positive class, mainly because of the various JPEG compression quality levels. However, the positive and negative scores are perfectly separated, suggesting a cutoff threshold of 0.07. That’s the value we set in the software. Robustness to Cropping and Rigid Rotations As you can see from the output table, the filter will detect the watermark even when the image has been rotated by multiples of 90 degrees and/or when it’s been cropped. In both cases, the estimated geometric transformation is also provided. As you can see from the output table, the filter will detect the watermark even when the image has been rotated by multiples of 90 degrees and/or when it’s been cropped. In both cases, the estimated geometrical transformation is also provided. The Raw Conversion Watermark Map filter Once you know an image contains the watermark globally, it makes good sense to check whether it’s present throughout the image or missing from specific regions. That could be justified by them being less capable of hosting the watermark (e.g. white- or black- saturated regions can hardly embed the watermark). More interestingly, its absence could be motivated by a local manipulation being applied to the image. This feature was already available since the previous update, but we renamed it by adding “Map” to the filter name. With this update, we’re also adding robustness to cropping and rigid rotations. So, if the image was processed in such a way as part of the tampering process, the forgery would still be detected. Annotate, Now with the Bezier Curve Option We’re bringing to Authenticate the ability to draw nice curved lines with the Annotate tool! To do so, just go to the Arrow tool as usual, enable the Bezier curve checkbox, and draw the arrow. You can then use the control points to obtain the curved effect. PRNU Create CRP: New Ability to Add Text Notes This new feature was implemented 100% thanks to you, dear Authenticate users! One of you told us that when creating the Camera Reference Pattern to work on a PRNU case, it would have been useful to write some notes associated with the CRP file, and have them retained in the associated CRP log file. And so… there you have it! Whatever you wrote above will be reported at the top of the .crp.log file that gets created. Improvement to Software Delivery Options Producing software goes beyond adding new features. It also involves how you ship it and how users can get it working. With this update, we’re adding two important updates on this side. Allow Documents Folders to Be Created Optionally When installing Authenticate, you’ll be offered the option to postpone the creation of the folders that are normally placed in the current user’s Documents folder. This allows completing the installation on setups having the Documents folder on a network path. You’ll then be able to enter the desired folder location in the Program Options, under the General Settings tab. AI or Not? The Choice Is Yours! At Amped, we strongly believe that the use of AI should never be imposed, but offered at most. As such, it should be a unit’s / agency’s decision whether AI systems should be offered to their members or not. To accommodate that, we are offering two versions of Authenticate from within the Support Portal . The AI-enabled version, which is the default one, includes tools based on AI, and the AI-free version does not include AI-based tools. All of that being said, if you’re an Amped user, you know how responsibly we deal with AI in our products. In Authenticate, every time a filter uses AI, this is printed in the GUI, the report, and in the filter manual, so as to make the user aware. Other Improvements Bookmarks Panel: Add Buttons to Move Bookmarks Up and Down Like in FIVE Yet another suggestion coming from our loved users! You can now arrange bookmarks using buttons and not just drag and drop! Add Label to Distinguish Among Internal, File System and Computed Metadata When accessing the File Format table, you’ll now see an additional column that clarifies where the information in each row originates from. For example, the Exif’s Modify Date is marked as “internal” because it’s stored inside the file. On the other hand, the “Last modification date” is stored outside the file, as the system’s metadata, and is therefore marked as “external”. Finally, the hash values are calculated by Authenticate, and are therefore marked as “computed”. Add Spell Checker to Bookmark Pop-up Typos can lower the perceived quality of an otherwise excellent report, and unfortunately they’re always around the corner! To help with that, we’ve now enabled the system’s spell checker to work in the bookmark description box. Smart Report: Add Ability to Select Report Format Type Another small but nice one: when using the Smart Report to triage your files, you’ll now be offered the option to use the same formats available for the standard report. Other Improvements and Bug Fixes We’ve made other improvements to the software, including: We unified the cache management for the Image and Video Modes, so the related controls are now available in the General tab of the Program Options. For the Video Mode, only the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter supports caching as of now. VPF : we updated the legend of values in the plot to better explain that they do not match the Macroblocks filter (see the manual for further details!). Batch File Format Analysis and Batch File Format Comparison : we’ve reorganized the columns, putting the most relevant information upfront and disabling some of the columns by default. You can always re-enable them by right-clicking on the top of the table as usual. We updated FFmpeg to version 8.1. We’ve improved the icon for the Rotate button in the Video Mode. We fixed a bug that caused the GPU not to be used when running the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter on images. Don’t Delay – Update Today The new features make Authenticate more powerful than ever. If you have an active support plan, you can update straight away by going into the menu About > Check for Updates within Amped Authenticate. If you need to renew your SMS plan, please contact us or one of our authorized distributors. And remember that you can always manage your license and requests from the Amped Support Portal . FAQ – Amped Authenticate Update Authenticate Update 43130 What’s new in Amped Authenticate Update 43130? Amped Authenticate Update 43130 introduces the Atom Viewer for analyzing MP4 and MOV video container structures, a new filter for global Adobe RAW conversion watermark detection, and improved forgery localization supporting cropping and rotations. Other additions include Bézier curve annotations, enhanced PRNU workflows, reporting improvements, and a new AI-free software version. How can the Atom Viewer help identify modifications to video files? The new Atom Viewer, available in Video Mode’s Advanced File Info tool, allows you to examine the internal structure of MP4-like video containers, including MOV files. By inspecting the organization of atoms, tracks, and metadata, you can identify structural differences that may indicate video processing or modification, even when conventional metadata does not reveal these changes. Can Amped Authenticate detect whether an image has been processed with Adobe Photoshop or Lightroom? Authenticate includes a Raw Conversion Watermark filter that detects the characteristic pattern introduced during certain Adobe Photoshop or Lightroom RAW conversion workflows. The filter uses a statistical, non-AI-based method to assess the watermark’s presence. A positive result indicates this processing history but does not, by itself, establish whether an image has been manipulated. What’s the difference between the Raw Conversion Watermark and Raw Conversion Watermark Map filters? The Raw Conversion Watermark filter performs global detection, checking whether the Adobe RAW conversion pattern is present in an image as a whole. The Raw Conversion Watermark Map filter examines its spatial distribution, helping you identify regions where the pattern is absent. Such inconsistencies may warrant further investigation for possible local manipulation. Can Amped Authenticate detect Adobe RAW watermark traces after an image has been cropped or rotated? Yes. This update improves the robustness of both watermark analysis filters to cropping and rotations by multiples of 90 degrees. The filters can account for these transformations when detecting the watermark or investigating possible local inconsistencies, helping you examine images that have undergone additional processing. Is Amped Authenticate available without AI-based tools? Yes. This update introduces an AI-free version alongside the standard AI-enabled version. Both are available through the Amped Support Portal, allowing you to choose whether to include AI-based analysis tools according to your operational requirements and internal policies. What improvements does Update 43130 bring to forensic reporting and documentation? The update introduces Bézier curve annotations, the ability to save notes in Camera Reference Pattern (CRP) log files, spell checking in bookmark descriptions, and additional Smart Report output formats. It also adds clearer labels distinguishing internal, file system, and computed metadata, supporting more transparent documentation of forensic findings. https://blog.ampedsoftware.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Authenticate-update-43130-1.png

One of you told us that when creating the Camera Reference Pattern to work on a PRNU case, it would have been useful to write some notes associated with the CRP file, and have them retained in the associated CRP log file.

And so… there you have it!

Whatever you wrote above will be reported at the top of the .crp.log file that gets created.

Improvement to Software Delivery Options

Producing software goes beyond adding new features. It also involves how you ship it and how users can get it working. With this update, we’re adding two important updates on this side.

Allow Documents Folders to Be Created Optionally

When installing Authenticate, you’ll be offered the option to postpone the creation of the folders that are normally placed in the current user’s Documents folder. This allows completing the installation on setups having the Documents folder on a network path. You’ll then be able to enter the desired folder location in the Program Options, under the General Settings tab.

AI or Not? The Choice Is Yours!

At Amped, we strongly believe that the use of AI should never be imposed, but offered at most. As such, it should be a unit’s / agency’s decision whether AI systems should be offered to their members or not.

To accommodate that, we are offering two versions of Authenticate from within the Support Portal. The AI-enabled version, which is the default one, includes tools based on AI, and the AI-free version does not include AI-based tools.

All of that being said, if you’re an Amped user, you know how responsibly we deal with AI in our products. In Authenticate, every time a filter uses AI, this is printed in the GUI, the report, and in the filter manual, so as to make the user aware.

Other Improvements Bookmarks Panel: Add Buttons to Move Bookmarks Up and Down Like in FIVE

Yet another suggestion coming from our loved users!

You can now arrange bookmarks using buttons and not just drag and drop!

Add Label to Distinguish Among Internal, File System and Computed Metadata

When accessing the File Format table, you’ll now see an additional column that clarifies where the information in each row originates from.

For example, the Exif’s Modify Date is marked as “internal” because it’s stored inside the file. On the other hand, the “Last modification date” is stored outside the file, as the system’s metadata, and is therefore marked as “external”. Finally, the hash values are calculated by Authenticate, and are therefore marked as “computed”.

Add Spell Checker to Bookmark Pop-up

Typos can lower the perceived quality of an otherwise excellent report, and unfortunately they’re always around the corner!

To help with that, we’ve now enabled the system’s spell checker to work in the bookmark description box.

Smart Report: Add Ability to Select Report Format Type

Another small but nice one: when using the Smart Report to triage your files, you’ll now be offered the option to use the same formats available for the standard report.

Other Improvements and Bug Fixes

We’ve made other improvements to the software, including:

  • We unified the cache management for the Image and Video Modes, so the related controls are now available in the General tab of the Program Options. For the Video Mode, only the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter supports caching as of now.
  • VPF: we updated the legend of values in the plot to better explain that they do not match the Macroblocks filter (see the manual for further details!).
  • Batch File Format Analysis and Batch File Format Comparison: we’ve reorganized the columns, putting the most relevant information upfront and disabling some of the columns by default. You can always re-enable them by right-clicking on the top of the table as usual.
  • We updated FFmpeg to version 8.1.
  • We’ve improved the icon for the Rotate button in the Video Mode.
  • We fixed a bug that caused the GPU not to be used when running the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter on images.

Don’t Delay – Update Today

The new features make Authenticate more powerful than ever.

If you have an active support plan, you can update straight away by going into the menu About > Check for Updates within Amped Authenticate. If you need to renew your SMS plan, please contact us or one of our authorized distributors. And remember that you can always manage your license and requests from the Amped Support Portal.

FAQ – Amped Authenticate Update Authenticate Update 43130

What’s new in Amped Authenticate Update 43130?

Amped Authenticate Update 43130 introduces the Atom Viewer for analyzing MP4 and MOV video container structures, a new filter for global Adobe RAW conversion watermark detection, and improved forgery localization supporting cropping and rotations. Other additions include Bézier curve annotations, enhanced PRNU workflows, reporting improvements, and a new AI-free software version.

How can the Atom Viewer help identify modifications to video files?

The new Atom Viewer, available in Video Mode’s Advanced File Info tool, allows you to examine the internal structure of MP4-like video containers, including MOV files. By inspecting the organization of atoms, tracks, and metadata, you can identify structural differences that may indicate video processing or modification, even when conventional metadata does not reveal these changes.

Can Amped Authenticate detect whether an image has been processed with Adobe Photoshop or Lightroom?

Authenticate includes a Raw Conversion Watermark filter that detects the characteristic pattern introduced during certain Adobe Photoshop or Lightroom RAW conversion workflows. The filter uses a statistical, non-AI-based method to assess the watermark’s presence. A positive result indicates this processing history but does not, by itself, establish whether an image has been manipulated.

What’s the difference between the Raw Conversion Watermark and Raw Conversion Watermark Map filters?

The Raw Conversion Watermark filter performs global detection, checking whether the Adobe RAW conversion pattern is present in an image as a whole. The Raw Conversion Watermark Map filter examines its spatial distribution, helping you identify regions where the pattern is absent. Such inconsistencies may warrant further investigation for possible local manipulation.

Can Amped Authenticate detect Adobe RAW watermark traces after an image has been cropped or rotated?

Yes. This update improves the robustness of both watermark analysis filters to cropping and rotations by multiples of 90 degrees. The filters can account for these transformations when detecting the watermark or investigating possible local inconsistencies, helping you examine images that have undergone additional processing.

Is Amped Authenticate available without AI-based tools?

Yes. This update introduces an AI-free version alongside the standard AI-enabled version. Both are available through the Amped Support Portal, allowing you to choose whether to include AI-based analysis tools according to your operational requirements and internal policies.

What improvements does Update 43130 bring to forensic reporting and documentation?

The update introduces Bézier curve annotations, the ability to save notes in Camera Reference Pattern (CRP) log files, spell checking in bookmark descriptions, and additional Smart Report output formats. It also adds clearer labels distinguishing internal, file system, and computed metadata, supporting more transparent documentation of forensic findings.
