items.title: Meta AI Agent Muse Reads Encrypted Messages Through Android Notifications and Mac Permissions
items.summary: Meta’s AI agent Muse read Signal message text on Android phones and Macs without directly connecting to the encrypted messaging app, Reuters reported on November 18. The investigation found that Muse could use Android notifications and macOS permissions to see text already displayed on a device. The tests did not show that Muse broke Signal’s end-to-end encryption . The finding followed an internal complaint from a Meta employee who said Muse unexpectedly reminded her to reply to a Signal message from her sister. The employee was using a personal phone and said she did not recall granting Muse access to other apps. A colleague said he traced similar reminders to Android notification access. The complaints surfaced after Muse, represented by a fuzzy mascot named Jolly, passed 10 million downloads following its September launch. Employees also reported unsolicited messages about childcare, career advice, and purchases they had not made. In one case, a routine update about fishing conditions included two bank balances the recipient did not recognize. Muse Read Signal Messages on Android and Mac On Android, Muse read message text from push notifications. Signal encrypts messages between devices, but a notification preview can display the text after it arrives. An app with notification access can see what appears in those alerts. That is different from opening Signal, reading its full chat history, or breaking its encryption. On macOS, testers found that Muse could use accessibility and screenshot tools to read Signal text. Neither the Android nor the Mac test required adding Signal through Meta’s Connector feature, which links external services to the assistant. The same request was blocked on the iPhone used in testing. The Reuters investigation highlights a distinction users can easily miss: leaving Signal off an agent’s list of connected apps does not revoke permissions granted through the operating system. Cybersecurity News previously covered a separate Apple notification privacy flaw that exposed Signal message text through a different route. In both cases, the exposure involved text the device had already received. Meta said Muse can access other apps only through permissions users explicitly grant. The company described the reported cases as isolated and said many suspected account mix-ups were AI hallucinations, meaning the assistant generated information that was not based on real records. The tests confirmed that Muse could read Signal text, but they did not establish that the bank figures belonged to another user. Mac users can check System Settings under Privacy & Security and remove Muse’s accessibility or screen recording access if they do not need those features. Cybersecurity News’ coverage of macOS 27.3 beta privacy controls explains why existing grants deserve a separate review: tighter controls do not necessarily remove access an app already has. Android users can search system settings for “Notification access” and turn off Muse’s access if it is enabled. They can also follow Signal’s notification settings guide to hide message text in alerts. The two changes do different things: hiding previews limits what Signal puts in a notification, while revoking access stops Muse from reading notifications through that permission. Neither requires turning off Signal notifications altogether, so users can still receive alerts without showing the message text. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!
items.summary_html:
Meta’s AI agent Muse read Signal message text on Android phones and Macs without directly connecting to the encrypted messaging app, Reuters reported on November 18.

The investigation found that Muse could use Android notifications and macOS permissions to see text already displayed on a device. The tests did not show that Muse broke Signal’s end-to-end encryption.

The finding followed an internal complaint from a Meta employee who said Muse unexpectedly reminded her to reply to a Signal message from her sister. The employee was using a personal phone and said she did not recall granting Muse access to other apps. A colleague said he traced similar reminders to Android notification access.

The complaints surfaced after Muse, represented by a fuzzy mascot named Jolly, passed 10 million downloads following its September launch.

Employees also reported unsolicited messages about childcare, career advice, and purchases they had not made. In one case, a routine update about fishing conditions included two bank balances the recipient did not recognize.

Muse Read Signal Messages on Android and Mac

On Android, Muse read message text from push notifications. Signal encrypts messages between devices, but a notification preview can display the text after it arrives.

An app with notification access can see what appears in those alerts. That is different from opening Signal, reading its full chat history, or breaking its encryption.

On macOS, testers found that Muse could use accessibility and screenshot tools to read Signal text. Neither the Android nor the Mac test required adding Signal through Meta’s Connector feature, which links external services to the assistant. The same request was blocked on the iPhone used in testing.

The Reuters investigation highlights a distinction users can easily miss: leaving Signal off an agent’s list of connected apps does not revoke permissions granted through the operating system.

Cybersecurity News previously covered a separate Apple notification privacy flaw that exposed Signal message text through a different route. In both cases, the exposure involved text the device had already received.

Meta said Muse can access other apps only through permissions users explicitly grant. The company described the reported cases as isolated and said many suspected account mix-ups were AI hallucinations, meaning the assistant generated information that was not based on real records. The tests confirmed that Muse could read Signal text, but they did not establish that the bank figures belonged to another user.

Mac users can check System Settings under Privacy & Security and remove Muse’s accessibility or screen recording access if they do not need those features.

Cybersecurity News’ coverage of macOS 27.3 beta privacy controls explains why existing grants deserve a separate review: tighter controls do not necessarily remove access an app already has.

Android users can search system settings for “Notification access” and turn off Muse’s access if it is enabled. They can also follow Signal’s notification settings guide to hide message text in alerts.

The two changes do different things: hiding previews limits what Signal puts in a notification, while revoking access stops Muse from reading notifications through that permission. Neither requires turning off Signal notifications altogether, so users can still receive alerts without showing the message text.

items.title: Pluralistic: How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (19 Nov 2026)
items.summary: Today's links How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies : Author beware, termination of transfer and loan-out companies don't mix! Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : History of interlibrary loan; Mike Pence v Hamilton; Snoopers' Charter is law; Teamsters transformed. Upcoming appearances : Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies ( permalink ) There's a seeming paradox to copyright. For 50 years (starting with the 1976 Copyright Act) legislatures have monotonically expanded copyright, so that today, copyright lasts longer, covers more works, restricts more activities, and provides for harsher penalties for infringement, all in the name of protecting artists. After 50 years of this, artists are, on average, poorer than we were in 1976, but the media companies we sell our work to are much, much richer. They're larger and more profitable, and yet our wealth (both in absolute terms and as a share of media company profits) has declined. This may feel like a paradox, but it's actually easy to understand unless you've had the self-inflicted neurological injury we call "getting an econ degree." That's an injury that leaves the sufferer incapable of reasoning about or even perceiving power . If you've avoided that fate, then you can see that when an artist sells to one of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies or one ebook/audiobook company, that artist has very little leverage. In that market, giving an artist more to bargain with is just giving them more to bargain away . I have often compared giving more copyright to creative workers trapped in this oligopoly to giving a bullied schoolchild extra lunch money. No matter how much money you give that kid, they're not going to get fed. The bullies just take whatever money you give to the kid. Indeed, if you indirectly transfer enough money to the bullies, they'll pay for a global ad campaign: THINK OF THE HUNGRY SCHOOLCHILDREN! THEY NEED MORE LUNCH MONEY! This is exactly what has happened with 50 years of successive copyright expansions. Every time Congress gave a new copyright to creative workers, the cartels we bargain with just amended their non-negotiable contracts to force us to hand over that new right for no extra payment. Then they used those new rights to get richer and more powerful, and to exert more control over the distribution channels we need to reach our audiences, which made us poorer. Then Congress heard their THINK OF THE STARVING ARTISTS pitch, and gave us more copyright…which we promptly handed over to our bosses. Lather, rinse, repeat. If you want to feed a hungry schoolkid, you have to change the structure of the system. For example, you might open a credit account with the school lunchroom, so that the kid never has any cash for the bullies to take. Likewise, if you want to help artists get more money, you need to make a systemic change. There are lots of ways to do this. In 2022, Rebecca Giblin and I co-wrote a book called Chokepoint Capitalism , and we devoted half of the book to detailed, shovel-ready proposals for ways to alter the copyright system to benefit artists, not our bosses: https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx That section includes a chapter on something called "termination of transfer," which was introduced with the 1976 Copyright Act. Under termination of transfer, any copyright contract (a "transfer") can be unilaterally canceled ("termination") by any creator after 35 years. So even if you sign away your copyrights for the entire term (your life plus 70 years), you can tear up that agreement after 35 years by notifying the company you sold your rights to and then filing some paperwork with the US Copyright Office: https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/ We got really excited about termination. For one thing, Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject. In 2021, she co-authored the landmark study "U.S. Copyright Termination Notices 1977-2020: Introducing New Datasets," published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies : https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708 Termination is a uniquely efficient way to make artists richer at the expense of our bosses. The fact that you can only exercise it after 35 years produces some very interesting effects. First, consider that almost no copyrighted works are commercially viable after 35 years (most copyrighted works cease to generate income after 14 years or less, this being the original term of copyright in the USA). The rare works that continue to generate revenue 35 years after their release are the "perennial favorites" that drive a vast share of media industry profits. Now consider that, between the realities of the human lifespan and the amount of time it takes most artists to master their craft, any given work you produced 35 years ago is almost certainly from the start of your career. That's the moment in which artists are typically most vulnerable. Artists at the start of their careers are unknown quantities and are often crammed into signing terrible deals, even worse than the "standard" media deal. Put these two facts together and you'll see that termination is disproportionately applicable to a body of work that is wildly profitable for media companies, but the creators of those works are entitled to even less of the money it generates, thanks to the crummy contracts they were railroaded into because they were just starting out when they made them. Termination lets creators cancel those crummy contracts, take back their rights, and bargain for a better deal with the old media company (or a new one). This time, they bargain from a position of unassailable strength, due to the fact that they're selling a property that's proven itself to be a perennial profit-generator. Best of all, you can't bargain out of termination. Even if you sign a contract that says, "I promise I will not exercise my termination of transfer right," you can still exercise your termination right. This is a structural change, like the parent who opens a charge account with the school cafeteria so that their kid no longer has any lunch money to hand over to the bullies. The way Congress wrote termination into the 1976 Act, it doesn't matter how hard the media company you initially sign with twists your arm, you literally can't promise them you won't use your termination right 35 years after signing. That's where that landmark study Rebecca co-authored comes in. Rebecca and her co-authors found that termination was working exactly the way Congress intended: it was making artists richer. It's particularly helpful to marginalized creative workers, for example, Black "heritage" musicians who were railroaded into terrible contracts that meant they never got a dime for decades of airplay, covers and samples of their hits. If this sounds familiar, you might be thinking of my 2024 technothriller The Bezzle , where I use this as a key plot point: https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/ Genre writers have really benefited from termination. The authors of massively popular YA series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High claimed back their rights under termination. So did Peter Straub and Stephen King, who took back the rights to their early books and resold them on much more favorable terms. Just the threat of termination forced Disney to make giant payouts to Marvel's key creators, like Stan Lee, Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby: https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/ In Chokepoint Capitalism , Rebecca and I point out that most of the 1976 Copyright Act (like longer copyright terms) has failed to help artists, but termination is the rare exception, a proven effective way to put money in artists' pockets. Which is weird, because in the 50 years since the 1976 Act, Congress has repeatedly doubled down on pretty much every measure in the Act, except the one thing that is empirically proven to be good for artists. Of course, all that failed stuff in the 1976 Act is good for giant media companies, and termination is bad for those companies, so it's not hard to see why there's been so little legislative appetite to beef up termination. But it's also easy to see how we'd do that beefing up. In the original draft of the Copyright Act, termination was automatic, and kicked in after 20 years (meaning that 20 years after signing any contract, every creator would automatically get back all the rights they sold in the contract). The final version of the Act watered down termination so it kicks in after 35 years, and even then only after the artist does a ton of paperwork. Giving artists the termination rights they were promised in the initial draft of the 1976 Act is a no-brainer. But that's not what we've gotten from Congress. To the extent that Congress acted on termination, it was to take it away from musicians. In 1999, an obscure Congressional staffer named Mitch Glazier snuck a clause into an unrelated bill that made it impossible for most recording artists to exercise their termination rights. This was such a scandal that Congress had to convene a special session to cancel this amendment and restore musicians' rights, and Glazier was drummed out of his Congressional job: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire Don't worry, Glazier landed on his feet: he was immediately hired by the RIAA (the record industry's lobbying arm) as their new CEO and there he perches even today, making more than $1.4m/year to do a job he continues to describe as "defending artists": https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037 With Glazier as the standard-bearer for "artists' rights," it's no wonder that creators haven't gotten a better deal on termination out of Congress. Indeed, things are looking very bad for termination of transfer right now, thanks to a string of court decisions that pit a common tax strategy employed by freelance creatives against termination of transfer. Like many freelancers, creative workers often incorporate limited liability companies that contract with the companies that employ them. These companies then pass the revenue on to creators as "partner distributions." There are lots of reasons to like this arrangement: it simplifies probate and estate planning, helps creators fund their pensions, and offers tax deductions for expenses like a home office or research trips. This arrangement is especially common in Hollywood, where the companies that writers, directors, and other creative trades work through are called "loan-out companies" (because the company employs the creative, and "loans them out" to movie studios). Movie studios and other media companies have recently seized on the existence of these loan-out companies to argue (with a great deal of success) that the existence of these loan-out companies nullifies termination of transfer. You see, termination of transfer is only available for creative works that are independently produced and licensed through a copyright contract. Termination does not apply to "works made for hire," such as the emails and reports you might write in the course of your duties as an employee. The logic here is that termination of transfer is supposed to help artists get more out of their copyrights, but forcing (say) an insurance company to disgorge all the memos you wrote for them 35 years ago would introduce chaos and uncertainty without helping workers in any way (there's not exactly a market for 35-year-old insurance company memos). The media companies' argument goes that creative workers are employees of their loan-out companies, so if you sell a script or a novel through your LLC, that is a "work made for hire" that the LLC owned, and that means that it can't exercise your termination of transfer rights to get that work back after 35 years. Aaron Moss, who edits the Copyright Lately website, has been beating the drum about this for years, calling it "a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries." He's been repeatedly vindicated, most recently through a bizarre dispute between Michael Mann, the director and writer of 1995's blockbuster Heat , and New Regency, the studio that released it: https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/ Moss's article on the dispute is a very entertaining read, unpacking a decidedly weird gambit that Mann has deployed to regain the rights to Heat . But the most important part of the article is the way it describes the state of play for termination's ongoing collision with loan-out companies. The studios and labels have racked up a string of wins using this gambit, with creators settling their cases or losing outright. Take musician John Waite's bid to get his rights back from UMG: the judge ruled in UMG's favor, saying, "people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes – eg taking advantage of tax benefits – and then disavow it for others": https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/ This is a bad situation. Termination is a fantastic, artist-friendly legal doctrine, one that lets creators claim back some of our most cherished media. Termination gave George Clinton the rights back to his entire catalog (his sleazy ex-manager forged Clinton's signature on a rights assignment). It let Gary K Wolf take Roger Rabbit back from Disney: https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way It let the Spinal Tap crew get a much better deal out of their studio, and paved the way for 2025's (criminally underrated) Spinal Tap II : https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087 The Wachowskis just announced that they're going to exercise their termination rights to get The Matrix back from Warner Brothers, which is now owned by Trump's cronies, thanks to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's decision to let the Warner-Paramount merger go through: https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix This clash between termination and loan-outs has been on my radar since 2021, when the artist-defending media lawyer Jeff Trexler told me about it over drinks at Comic-Con. I've since spoken to accountants and lawyers who think there might be a way to finesse this if creators set up contracts with their loan-outs that give the loan-outs the right to collect their royalties and advances, without assigning copyright to the loan-out companies. I don't have any definitive answers on this: if you're worried about it, you should talk to your own lawyers and accountants. It's a dangerous erosion of one of the few bright spots in copyright, a rule that is an unambiguously good way to benefit artists, not media companies. In the meantime, if you've got some 35-year-old copyrights you'd like to terminate, I've got a tip for you. The Authors Alliance is a nonprofit that defends the rights of authors (I volunteer for its advisory board); we've got a free online tool that will help you terminate your own transfers and get your How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (permalink)

There's a seeming paradox to copyright. For 50 years (starting with the 1976 Copyright Act) legislatures have monotonically expanded copyright, so that today, copyright lasts longer, covers more works, restricts more activities, and provides for harsher penalties for infringement, all in the name of protecting artists.

After 50 years of this, artists are, on average, poorer than we were in 1976, but the media companies we sell our work to are much, much richer. They're larger and more profitable, and yet our wealth (both in absolute terms and as a share of media company profits) has declined.

This may feel like a paradox, but it's actually easy to understand unless you've had the self-inflicted neurological injury we call "getting an econ degree." That's an injury that leaves the sufferer incapable of reasoning about or even perceiving power.

If you've avoided that fate, then you can see that when an artist sells to one of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies or one ebook/audiobook company, that artist has very little leverage. In that market, giving an artist more to bargain with is just giving them more to bargain away.

I have often compared giving more copyright to creative workers trapped in this oligopoly to giving a bullied schoolchild extra lunch money. No matter how much money you give that kid, they're not going to get fed. The bullies just take whatever money you give to the kid. Indeed, if you indirectly transfer enough money to the bullies, they'll pay for a global ad campaign: THINK OF THE HUNGRY SCHOOLCHILDREN! THEY NEED MORE LUNCH MONEY!

This is exactly what has happened with 50 years of successive copyright expansions. Every time Congress gave a new copyright to creative workers, the cartels we bargain with just amended their non-negotiable contracts to force us to hand over that new right for no extra payment. Then they used those new rights to get richer and more powerful, and to exert more control over the distribution channels we need to reach our audiences, which made us poorer. Then Congress heard their THINK OF THE STARVING ARTISTS pitch, and gave us more copyright…which we promptly handed over to our bosses. Lather, rinse, repeat.

If you want to feed a hungry schoolkid, you have to change the structure of the system. For example, you might open a credit account with the school lunchroom, so that the kid never has any cash for the bullies to take. Likewise, if you want to help artists get more money, you need to make a systemic change.

There are lots of ways to do this. In 2022, Rebecca Giblin and I co-wrote a book called Chokepoint Capitalism, and we devoted half of the book to detailed, shovel-ready proposals for ways to alter the copyright system to benefit artists, not our bosses:

https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx

That section includes a chapter on something called "termination of transfer," which was introduced with the 1976 Copyright Act. Under termination of transfer, any copyright contract (a "transfer") can be unilaterally canceled ("termination") by any creator after 35 years. So even if you sign away your copyrights for the entire term (your life plus 70 years), you can tear up that agreement after 35 years by notifying the company you sold your rights to and then filing some paperwork with the US Copyright Office:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/

We got really excited about termination. For one thing, Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject. In 2021, she co-authored the landmark study "U.S. Copyright Termination Notices 1977-2020: Introducing New Datasets," published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies:

https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708

Termination is a uniquely efficient way to make artists richer at the expense of our bosses. The fact that you can only exercise it after 35 years produces some very interesting effects. First, consider that almost no copyrighted works are commercially viable after 35 years (most copyrighted works cease to generate income after 14 years or less, this being the original term of copyright in the USA). The rare works that continue to generate revenue 35 years after their release are the "perennial favorites" that drive a vast share of media industry profits.

Now consider that, between the realities of the human lifespan and the amount of time it takes most artists to master their craft, any given work you produced 35 years ago is almost certainly from the start of your career. That's the moment in which artists are typically most vulnerable. Artists at the start of their careers are unknown quantities and are often crammed into signing terrible deals, even worse than the "standard" media deal.

Put these two facts together and you'll see that termination is disproportionately applicable to a body of work that is wildly profitable for media companies, but the creators of those works are entitled to even less of the money it generates, thanks to the crummy contracts they were railroaded into because they were just starting out when they made them.

Termination lets creators cancel those crummy contracts, take back their rights, and bargain for a better deal with the old media company (or a new one). This time, they bargain from a position of unassailable strength, due to the fact that they're selling a property that's proven itself to be a perennial profit-generator.

Best of all, you can't bargain out of termination. Even if you sign a contract that says, "I promise I will not exercise my termination of transfer right," you can still exercise your termination right. This is a structural change, like the parent who opens a charge account with the school cafeteria so that their kid no longer has any lunch money to hand over to the bullies. The way Congress wrote termination into the 1976 Act, it doesn't matter how hard the media company you initially sign with twists your arm, you literally can't promise them you won't use your termination right 35 years after signing.

That's where that landmark study Rebecca co-authored comes in. Rebecca and her co-authors found that termination was working exactly the way Congress intended: it was making artists richer. It's particularly helpful to marginalized creative workers, for example, Black "heritage" musicians who were railroaded into terrible contracts that meant they never got a dime for decades of airplay, covers and samples of their hits. If this sounds familiar, you might be thinking of my 2024 technothriller The Bezzle, where I use this as a key plot point:

https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/

Genre writers have really benefited from termination. The authors of massively popular YA series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High claimed back their rights under termination. So did Peter Straub and Stephen King, who took back the rights to their early books and resold them on much more favorable terms. Just the threat of termination forced Disney to make giant payouts to Marvel's key creators, like Stan Lee, Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby:

https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/

In Chokepoint Capitalism, Rebecca and I point out that most of the 1976 Copyright Act (like longer copyright terms) has failed to help artists, but termination is the rare exception, a proven effective way to put money in artists' pockets. Which is weird, because in the 50 years since the 1976 Act, Congress has repeatedly doubled down on pretty much every measure in the Act, except the one thing that is empirically proven to be good for artists. Of course, all that failed stuff in the 1976 Act is good for giant media companies, and termination is bad for those companies, so it's not hard to see why there's been so little legislative appetite to beef up termination.

But it's also easy to see how we'd do that beefing up. In the original draft of the Copyright Act, termination was automatic, and kicked in after 20 years (meaning that 20 years after signing any contract, every creator would automatically get back all the rights they sold in the contract). The final version of the Act watered down termination so it kicks in after 35 years, and even then only after the artist does a ton of paperwork.

Giving artists the termination rights they were promised in the initial draft of the 1976 Act is a no-brainer. But that's not what we've gotten from Congress. To the extent that Congress acted on termination, it was to take it away from musicians. In 1999, an obscure Congressional staffer named Mitch Glazier snuck a clause into an unrelated bill that made it impossible for most recording artists to exercise their termination rights. This was such a scandal that Congress had to convene a special session to cancel this amendment and restore musicians' rights, and Glazier was drummed out of his Congressional job:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire

Don't worry, Glazier landed on his feet: he was immediately hired by the RIAA (the record industry's lobbying arm) as their new CEO and there he perches even today, making more than $1.4m/year to do a job he continues to describe as "defending artists":

https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037

With Glazier as the standard-bearer for "artists' rights," it's no wonder that creators haven't gotten a better deal on termination out of Congress.

Indeed, things are looking very bad for termination of transfer right now, thanks to a string of court decisions that pit a common tax strategy employed by freelance creatives against termination of transfer.

Like many freelancers, creative workers often incorporate limited liability companies that contract with the companies that employ them. These companies then pass the revenue on to creators as "partner distributions." There are lots of reasons to like this arrangement: it simplifies probate and estate planning, helps creators fund their pensions, and offers tax deductions for expenses like a home office or research trips.

This arrangement is especially common in Hollywood, where the companies that writers, directors, and other creative trades work through are called "loan-out companies" (because the company employs the creative, and "loans them out" to movie studios).

Movie studios and other media companies have recently seized on the existence of these loan-out companies to argue (with a great deal of success) that the existence of these loan-out companies nullifies termination of transfer.

You see, termination of transfer is only available for creative works that are independently produced and licensed through a copyright contract. Termination does not apply to "works made for hire," such as the emails and reports you might write in the course of your duties as an employee. The logic here is that termination of transfer is supposed to help artists get more out of their copyrights, but forcing (say) an insurance company to disgorge all the memos you wrote for them 35 years ago would introduce chaos and uncertainty without helping workers in any way (there's not exactly a market for 35-year-old insurance company memos).

The media companies' argument goes that creative workers are employees of their loan-out companies, so if you sell a script or a novel through your LLC, that is a "work made for hire" that the LLC owned, and that means that it can't exercise your termination of transfer rights to get that work back after 35 years.

Aaron Moss, who edits the Copyright Lately website, has been beating the drum about this for years, calling it "a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries." He's been repeatedly vindicated, most recently through a bizarre dispute between Michael Mann, the director and writer of 1995's blockbuster Heat, and New Regency, the studio that released it:

https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/

Moss's article on the dispute is a very entertaining read, unpacking a decidedly weird gambit that Mann has deployed to regain the rights to Heat. But the most important part of the article is the way it describes the state of play for termination's ongoing collision with loan-out companies. The studios and labels have racked up a string of wins using this gambit, with creators settling their cases or losing outright. Take musician John Waite's bid to get his rights back from UMG: the judge ruled in UMG's favor, saying, "people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes – eg taking advantage of tax benefits – and then disavow it for others":

https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/

This is a bad situation. Termination is a fantastic, artist-friendly legal doctrine, one that lets creators claim back some of our most cherished media. Termination gave George Clinton the rights back to his entire catalog (his sleazy ex-manager forged Clinton's signature on a rights assignment). It let Gary K Wolf take Roger Rabbit back from Disney:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way

It let the Spinal Tap crew get a much better deal out of their studio, and paved the way for 2025's (criminally underrated) Spinal Tap II:

https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087

The Wachowskis just announced that they're going to exercise their termination rights to get The Matrix back from Warner Brothers, which is now owned by Trump's cronies, thanks to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's decision to let the Warner-Paramount merger go through:

https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix

This clash between termination and loan-outs has been on my radar since 2021, when the artist-defending media lawyer Jeff Trexler told me about it over drinks at Comic-Con. I've since spoken to accountants and lawyers who think there might be a way to finesse this if creators set up contracts with their loan-outs that give the loan-outs the right to collect their royalties and advances, without assigning copyright to the loan-out companies. I don't have any definitive answers on this: if you're worried about it, you should talk to your own lawyers and accountants.

It's a dangerous erosion of one of the few bright spots in copyright, a rule that is an unambiguously good way to benefit artists, not media companies.

In the meantime, if you've got some 35-year-old copyrights you'd like to terminate, I've got a tip for you. The Authors Alliance is a nonprofit that defends the rights of authors (I volunteer for its advisory board); we've got a free online tool that will help you terminate your own transfers and get your rights back:

https://www.authorsalliance.org/resources/termination-of-transfer/

items.title: 3 New Tools: The Steam Queue, A Steam Page Checker, and how to make A Steam Page
items.summary: Tool #1: The Steam approval queue will take a month? Be warned, if you want to launch a Steam Page, launch a demo, or release a game, it is going to take at least a month (for now). Current wait is 47 days for a new Steamworks Verified account and 15 days for a build. AI generated everything has been pushing into day to day life and exhausting our human run systems in the weirdest places. Even a digital toy store like Steam. Reports are scattered and devs are left refreshing their inboxes, waiting for approval. It delayed the launch of several games including Rami Ismail’s game Australia Did It. So I built a tool to help. If you are stuck in the queue, you can share your numbers and see how stuck everyone else is. Bask in the conviviality of limbo. If you just about to release a game, check this site to see how long it will take you: The Steam Approval Queue Tracker What a strange time to be alive. Tool #2: HowToMakeASteamPage.com I just updated my original free course. It is still free. It is still about how to make a Steam page. I also replaced the old page art with beautiful new hand-made art from Jon Nielsen . Check it out: HowToMakeASteamPage.com Tool #2a: Steam page contest To celebrate the new course, I am running a contest. I am randomly picking 3 Steam pages from a qualified pool of applicants. If you want to throw your game in for consideration, join HowToMakeASteamPage.com and look for the first lecture and click there to enter . Tool #3: Steam page checker I see a lot of common mistakes with Steam pages that are just simple fixes. To help people identify these issues, I built a tool where you enter your Steam page URL and it flags common problems. The tool also links back to the Steam page course to explain how to fix the issue. To test your Steam page, go here: HowToMakeASteamPage.com

items.title: BADBOX 3.0 Malware Infects Android TV Boxes to Generate 40 Billion Fraudulent Ad Requests Daily
items.summary: Low-cost Android streaming boxes helped power an advertising fraud operation that generated roughly 40 billion bid requests a day at its peak. Known as BADBOX 3.0, the campaign used infected devices to play video ads outside the visible screen while making the traffic look as though it came from legitimate streaming apps. Some of the fraud did not require a real device at all. The figure measures requests to bid on advertising space, not ads watched, payments made, or devices infected. At its peak, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for more than 4% of the connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform. Its daily bid volume was more than three times that of VASTFLUX, the previous record holder cited in the research. Researchers from HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team identified and disrupted BADBOX 3.0, publishing their findings on November 18, 2026. items.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
items.summary: Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026. Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States. These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year. Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project , Cloudflare for Campaigns , and Project Galileo . Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups. Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026. In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings. Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period. State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information. On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second. Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone. Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data. Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools. Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks. PHP vulnerability On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell ) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability. On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend. Recommendations Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted. Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations: Prepare for surges in user traffic . Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff. Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure. Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules , to ensure new protections deploy by default. Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority. State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

Delphi language support is now built into SonarQube
items.summary: It’s an exciting day for us here at Sonar when we get to announce a new programming language! SonarQube Cloud now supports the Delphi programming language, including security rules and secrets detection for Delphi to help you comply with Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) . It includes the same maintainability rules, pull request and branch analysis, and quality gate pass/fail information in comments of your pull requests you already use for other languages, bringing Delphi in line with the other 45+ languages SonarQube supports . While Delphi is new for SonarQube , it is not a new language, with significant banking, manufacturing, and healthcare applications running on it. These applications are often very long lived with only a small group of developers keeping them going. The code gets harder to review as there are fewer people around with Delphi experience. This is where SonarQube can help with guidance on every PR to ensure your coding standards are met and the code keeps working. Where Delphi analysis stood before Delphi analysis in SonarQube came from the sonar-delphi community plugin. It was built over years with Delphi developers, and has more than 150 rules, and scans over 540 million lines of code on SonarQube Server. However, the plugin does not include security analysis. For teams with audit and compliance requirements, that meant the plugin wouldn’t completely satisfy their needs. What’s new This release adds security rules and secrets scanning, so security and compliance teams can now point to consistent results for their reporting and compliance attestation. Delphi analysis also behaves the same way as all of the other languages SonarQube supports. Automate pull request and branch analysis, quality gates in your CI pipeline to prevent substandard code from releasing, quality profiles to define your coding standards, and pass/fail results in the comments of pull request, so platform teams no longer need to manage a separate process for Delphi in a mixed-language setup. If your team is using AI assistants to cover Delphi, it works with Sonar Vortex too. Most coding agents have seen very little Delphi, and Vortex helps improve the quality of what they write before the code reaches review. Availability Native Delphi support is available now in SonarQube Cloud Enterprise plan.

items.title: SonarQube container scanning is now generally available
items.summary: Your code, your dependencies and your images, in one unified workflow In October, we opened the container scanning beta on a simple premise: the software you ship is more than the code in your repository. Today, container scanning is generally available in SonarQube Advanced Security on SonarQube Cloud. The timing matters. Yesterday, Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder, and fixes were released the same day. It arrives weeks after PHP2Shell. Neither flaw is in code your team wrote or a library you declared. Both live in the runtime inside your container images. A scan of your code and a scan of your dependencies can both come back clean while the vulnerable runtime ships. That gap is why container scanning belongs in the same workflow as everything else you verify: The code you write , analyzed by SonarQube. The dependencies you import , covered by SonarQube Advanced Security. The images you ship , now covered by container scanning. These are one application, and a risk in any layer is your risk. With container scanning, image findings appear next to code issues and dependency risks. They are triaged the same way and can fail the same CI build. You get one place to look and one process to run, and one answer when someone asks, “Are we exposed?” Let’s look at how you can use container scanning to detect images that contain Java4Shell vulnerability. What happened Java4Shell is a heap overflow in the optimized Base64 decoder that HotSpot uses on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support (Intel Ice Lake or newer, AMD Zen 4 or newer). A remote attacker who can get a crafted Base64 value into a vulnerable Java process can corrupt heap memory, and Calif demonstrated remote code execution without authentication in several widely used applications and frameworks. Base64 decoding is routine in server software, so ordinary features such as authentication can reach the vulnerable code. OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later is affected. Why your code and dependency scans will not see it Code analysis and dependency analysis will not show this flaw. It sits in the Java runtime underneath your code, not in your code or your declared libraries. Container scanning in SonarQube Advanced Security looks at the runtime itself. It matches each image against Linux distribution advisories and it re-checks images you have already scanned based on your organization's re-analysis settings so you do not need to scan them again. Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine have already published their advisories for CVE-2026-114938. Red Hat has a security bulletin and is preparing updates. How to check your images Run the Sonar container scanner on every image that includes a JDK or JRE, locally or in CI.Set your organization and token as environment variables first, so the token doesn’t appear in your command history, logs or process listings export SONAR_CONTAINER_SCANNER_ORG= export SONAR_CONTAINER_SCANNER_TOKEN= sonar-container-scanner Results appear in SonarQube Cloud under Container images . Images scanned after the CVE was published show it as soon as the scan completes. For images you analyzed earlier, SonarQube Cloud re-checks them for newly published vulnerabilities based on your organization’s re-analysis settings. 1. See which Java versions you run Screenshot 1. One repository, one row per scanned tag. What it shows. The eclipse-temurin repository with its three scanned tags, 25-jre, 21-jre and 17-jre. Each tag is its own scan, with a scan digest, the time of its last analysis, the number of risks (106, 240 and 240) and the most severe risk, which is Medium for all three. Use it to compare JDK lines side by side and open the tag you run in production. 2. Find every Java image in your organization Screenshot 2. Every image repository you have scanned, newest first. What it shows. The organization-wide Container images list: repository, time of last analysis, last scanned tag, risk count and most severe risk. The most recently scanned entries are Java images, java4shell-demo (debian-openjdk21, 193 risks), amazoncorretto (21, 4 risks) and eclipse-temurin (25-jre, 106 risks), with the other repositories below. Start here to pick out the images that carry a JDK. 3. Spot the JDK flaw among the other risks in an image Screenshot 3. The JDK risk sits in the same list as operating system package risks. What it shows. The eclipse-temurin 21-jre tag with 240 risks across 148 dependencies, sorted by severity. CVE-2026-114938 appears against oracle/openjdk 21.0.13+9-LTS as a direct runtime dependency with a CVSS score of 8.1 (High), alongside Ubuntu package advisories such as libsqlite3 and libgssapi. Use the search box to look up the CVE, the filters to narrow by risk type or severity, and the status and assignee controls on each row to start triage. 4. Read the risk and decide what to do Screenshot 4. The detail page for the Java4Shell risk. What it shows. The detail page for CVE-2026-114938, a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) published on November 17, 2026, with the affected dependency, oracle/openjdk 21.0.13+9-LTS, in the side panel. The page shows the severity, the status (Open, with a Change status button), an assignee, the CVSS score and whether the CVE is on the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, which it is not in this screenshot, plus a chance-of-exploitation section. The tabs, What’s the risk, How can I fix it and Activity, take you from the description to remediation and the history of the risk. Fix it Update the JDK. Rebuild each affected image on a base image with a patched OpenJDK, or update the vendor package, then push the new image. Scan the rebuilt image and confirm CVE-2026-114938 no longer appears under its risks. Add the scanner to CI with --fail-on high , or a threshold you choose, so a vulnerable runtime cannot ship again unnoticed. Java4Shell follows PHP2Shell: two critical flaws in a runtime inside your images within weeks. Both are invisible to code and dependency scans, and both show up when you scan the image. Try it today. Container scanning is part of SonarQube Advanced Security on SonarQube Cloud. How do I get started? You need: a SonarQube Cloud organization with SonarQube Advanced Security; a SonarQube Cloud user token; and the image available locally or in CI. Download the scanner for your platform from the scanner download page and follow the install steps in the documentation. Then set your organization and token as environment variables, so the token doesn’t appear in logs or process listings, and run the scanner: export SONAR_CONTAINER_SCANNER_ORG= export SONAR_CONTAINER_SCANNER_TOKEN= sonar-container-scanner By default, the scanner fails your build when it finds risks of high severity or above. Use --fail-on to change the threshold, for example to stop on medium risks too: docker build -t my-app:${BUILD_TAG} . sonar-container-scanner my-app:${BUILD_TAG} --fail-on medium The container scanning documentation covers CI secrets, supported image inputs, caching and every option. What do you see in SonarQube Cloud? Select Container images in the sidebar of your organization to see every image you have analyzed, with its tag, number of risks, most severe risk and when it was last analyzed. Open an image to see its versions and their risks, and manage them with the same workflow you use for dependency risks in your projects. When an image itself changes, run the scanner again to refresh its results. Why use SonarQube for container scanning? SonarQube is the independent code verification and governance platform for the code you write, the dependencies you import, and the images you ship. It doesn’t depend on any one cloud, model or agent vendor. For container images, that means: One place for all of it. Image risks sit next to your code and dependency risks, in the same workflow. Checks where developers build. Run it locally or in CI, and stop a risky image before it ships. An inventory that stays current. Every image version you analyze is re-checked as new vulnerabilities are published. Availability Container scanning is generally available on SonarQube Cloud for organizations with SonarQube Advanced Security on the Team or Enterprise plan, at no additional cost. Support for SonarQube Server is planned. Try it today Read the container scanning docs and run your first scan on an image you already build. New to SonarQube Advanced Security? Start a free trial .

items.summary: Key takeaways Registration is open for Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 (February 8-11), with 50+ presentations on AI, mobile, cloud, deepfakes, eDiscovery, incident response and more. Take part in content that is practical, including keynotes from Theresa Payton on AI, Scott Tillema on communicating and influencing under pressure, and Miguel Clarke on moving forensics from post-incident response to prevention. Attendees can compete in the three-hour Capture the Flag on Thursday, February 11 (powered by Hexordia), put questions to Magnet Forensics experts in live Q&A sessions, and see new Unpacked episodes. Magnet Virtual Summit is back February 8-11. This free event is where ideas advance digital investigations — your chance to learn what’s next from experts and peers, all in one place. Over four days, 50+ presentations will cover AI, mobile forensics, cloud investigations, deepfakes, eDiscovery, incident response and more. We’ll have special keynote presentations from our Co-Founder Jad Saliba, Theresa Payton, First Female White House Chief Information Officer, as well as FBI officers, Scott Tillema and Miguel Clarke. You’ll also learn more about the latest innovations from Magnet Forensics, including how Magnet One brings investigations together in one connected case workflow and how Magnet AI helps you turn digital evidence into investigative intelligence. The goal is to help you build stronger cases and solve them faster. Whatever your skill level, you’ll find something to move your work forward. Learn more below and register for the event here . What you can expect at the event MVS keynote presentations We’re excited to welcome three special guest keynote presenters for Magnet Virtual Summit 2027, in addition to our keynote presentation from Magnet Forensics leadership: Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 Welcome address: Intelligence in every digital investigation Jad Saliba, Co-Founder & Board Member, Magnet Forensics Kick off Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 with Magnet Forensics Co-Founder Jad Saliba! Jad will set the stage for the conversations happening across the Summit, including how public safety agencies are tackling growing backlogs, accessing evidence from vehicles and drones, and adopting AI responsibly while keeping findings defensible. Private sector teams will hear how incident response, insider threats, and internal investigations are changing as corporate data spreads across cloud platforms and distributed workforces. Throughout, Jad will share how Magnet Forensics is responding, from bringing investigations together in one connected case to turning digital evidence into investigative intelligence faster. Jad will also preview what’s ahead at Magnet Virtual Summit, including what to expect from our always popular Capture the Flag (CTF) competition, details of our interactive sessions, and some of the themes the 50+ speakers will explore in their presentations. The session will wrap up with a live Q&A, giving attendees a chance to engage directly with members of the Magnet Forensics team as Magnet Virtual Summit begins. Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 keynote: AI and the future of us: Navigating the promise and perils of artificial intelligence MVS keynote presenter: Theresa Payton, former White House CIO and leading expert in cybersecurity Few technological developments of the last century have fueled as much curiosity, misinformation and fear as AI. In this highly-engaging, jargon-free presentation, Theresa unpacks AI’s transformative power while exposing its looming risks, then demonstrates how our businesses, security and individual daily lives are being impacted by them. With anonymized stories from law enforcement’s front lines and stunning live demonstrations that reveal the tradecraft of modern cybercriminals, Theresa will equip you with practical actions to harness AI’s vast potential while protecting yourself, your clients and your organization. Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 keynote: The power of influence: Communicating when it matters most MVS keynote presenter: Scott Tillema, FBI-Trained Swat Hostage Negotiator What does it take to influence an outcome when emotions are high, trust is critical, and the stakes are significant? Drawing on gripping stories from his career as a SWAT hostage negotiator, Scott Tillema takes audiences inside the world of high-stakes negotiation to reveal the principles behind effective communication and influence. He translates these experiences into practical strategies for navigating difficult conversations, building trust, overcoming resistance, and influencing better outcomes when it matters most. Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 keynote: From evidence to foresight: Wisdom from the front lines of high-profile cyber incidents MVS keynote presenter: Miguel Clarke, Special Agent (retired), FBI In most organizations, digital forensics is treated as a post-incident service — called in after the damage is done. Yet the same expertise that reconstructs what happened can also help prevent it, limit its impact, and accelerate recovery. Drawing on 24 years with the FBI, including the 9/11 digital forensics investigation and the United States v. Pok Seong Kwong insider threat case cited in the third edition of Digital Evidence and Computer Crime, this keynote examines how seasoned examiners can apply their investigative insight to strengthen cybersecurity posture before the breach ever occurs. This session will present real world case analysis and operational lessons, showing how forensics professionals can move from being responders to being strategic partners in resilience — making their organizations safer, faster to recover, and better prepared for the next incident. Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 keynote: The DFIR investigative system MVS keynote presenter: Brett Shavers, Digital Forensics Consultant, DFIR Training Digital investigations are often treated as a sequence of technical steps, but an investigation is more than a workflow. It is a system. That system includes evidence, tools, the investigator, legal authority, scope, assumptions, hypotheses, attribution, peer review, reporting, and the decisions made between each step. Special brand-new Unpacked episodes Mobile Unpacked // Finding treasure — Using BFU data as our map to data Chris Vance, Senior Technical Forensics Specialist, Magnet Forensics Thanks to the use of file-based encryption in Android and Apple’s data protection, data becomes available at different times during a phone’s operation. While the bulk of information we want is protected by the user’s passcode, more information than meets the eye is waiting for us in the BFU state. This session will cover what information can be recovered from BFU extractions on both iOS and Android and how we can use this information to lead us to other ways to get the information. Cyber Unpacked // ATT&CK everywhere: Mapping adversary behavior across Windows, Linux and Mac in Magnet Axiom Cyber Doug Metz, Senior Security Forensics Specialist, Magnet Forensics MITRE ATT&CK gives investigators a common language for adversary behavior. Applying it consistently across every system in a modern environment has been harder. In this episode of Cyber Unpacked, we take a fresh look at how Axiom Cyber maps evidence to ATT&CK techniques across Windows and Linux, and we introduce the new support for macOS. We’ll walk through how Axiom Cyber matches artifacts to tactics and techniques and how to use those results to build a timeline of an intrusion, then show what Mac coverage adds to cross-platform investigations. We’ll also cover how to extend detection past the built-in rules by adding other Sigma rule repositories, whether that’s community projects, threat intel feeds or your team’s own rules, so your analysis can keep up with current threats. AI Unpacked // The state of AI at Magnet Forensics Brandon Epstein, Forensic Consultant, Magnet Forensics Patho Ghosh, VP, AI Products, Magnet Forensics Gabriel Fiorenzano Senior Product Manager, Magnet Forensics As AI evolves in all aspects of society, Magnet continues to lead the way in innovate AI in digital evidence and investigations. Brandon kicks off season 3 of AI Unpacked with the leaders at the forefront of AI feature development at Magnet Forensics to get the latest updates, views, and information on AI in our products today as well as a glimpse into the future of AI in DFIR. Legal Unpacked // The warrant and the clock: Digital search and seizure after Chatrie and Holcomb Justin Fitzsimmons, Technical Prosecutor Lead, Magnet Forensics and Chris Vance, Senior Technical Forensics Specialist, Magnet Forensics Where may investigators look, when must they stop, and what can they preserve while seeking a warrant? This webinar examines the changing boundaries of digital search and seizure through Chatrie, Holcomb, and the challenges of vanishing data. We’ll explore geolocation and cell tower warrants, particularity and search scope, and the consequences when recovered evidence undermines probable cause. The discussion will also distinguish device seizure, evidence preservation, and forensic examination, addressing the legal basis for timely action before data disappears or becomes inaccessible. Throughout, practical examples will connect these issues to warrant drafting, communication between attorneys and examiners, and documenting the facts that support each investigative step. Other MVS presentation highlights Four clocks, one second: Proving DC persistence from memory alone Andrew Kinsel, Cybersecurity Specialist, Levi, Ray & Shoup When the only evidence is a single memory image, how far can an investigation truly reach? This session reconstructs a real-world domain controller compromise entirely from RAM using MemProcFS, with no disk image or event logs. Starting from a YARA hit on a Tuoni C2 implant masquerading as placeholder.exe, it traces the process to a SYSTEM-level service persistence, then fixes the install moment to the second using four independent in-memory sources while ruling out timestamp tampering. The talk is candid about memory’s limits: why initial access often predates the captured image, and how a quiet timeline reflects eviction, not attacker inactivity. A concurrent OneDrive sync-log artifact on a second host models the discipline of separating a lead from a finding. Attendees leave with a repeatable MemProcFS triage workflow and a practical framework for multi-source temporal corroboration and validation checks. Winning leadership support: A playbook from two majors Ed O’Carroll, Major (retired), Fairfax County, VA Police Dept Ricky Johnson, Major of Criminal Investigations, Richland County Sheriff’s Dep Strong digital forensics programs require more than skilled examiners and advanced tools — they require informed, committed leadership. In this session, an active sheriff’s department major and a retired police major share practical strategies for gaining executive support, aligning digital forensics with agency priorities, and clearly communicating operational needs, risks, and return on investment. Attendees will learn how to build a compelling case for staffing, training, technology, policy development, and sustainable growth. Drawing on current and former executive leadership experience, the two presenters will provide a practical playbook for turning technical challenges into agency priorities that strengthen investigations, improve case outcomes, and better serve victims. Hiding in the shadows: A case study of Canada’s largest defamation case Ryan Duquette, Partner – National Leader of Digital Forensics, EY Think your snarky online comments are harmless? Move over Netflix dramas, this real-life courtroom saga has it all: villains, victims, Norwich Orders and digital forensics. What started as online trash-talk turned into Canada’s juiciest defamation case. One Toronto man found out the hard way that cyber-shade can cost more than a luxury condo. His keyboard antics led to a $4.7 million smackdown. Join us as we dive into this digital drama where trolling met its match — and the ‘post’ button proved pricier than anyone imagined. Grab your popcorn, we’re about to spill the digital tea. Standing up in court: Surviving Daubert challenges in digital forensics Jessica Hyde, Founder, Hexordia In modern digital investigations, examiners rely on a constantly evolving ecosystem of commercial, open-source, and custom scripts to extract critical artifact data. However, as legal scrutinies intensify, forensic findings are increasingly challenged under the Daubert standard — questioning whether tools are peer-reviewed, tested, and known to have acceptable error rates. How do we address AI based tooling with regards to Daubert? This session explores how practitioners can bridge the gap between fast-paced technological artifact analysis and courtroom admissibility. Attendees will walk through real-world case studies of artifact challenges, review key legal factors surrounding forensic methodology, and learn actionable steps to build defense-grade forensic reporting that withstands aggressive cross-examination. Your forensic report is going to be cross-examined: Are you ready? Sara Kurtzberg, Chief of Prosecutorial Innovation, Brooklyn District Attorneys Office A forensic report may be technically accurate and still create problems on the witness stand. Months, or sometimes years, after an examination is completed, a forensic examiner may be asked to explain tool versions, settings, validation procedures, missing artifacts, alternative interpretations, documentation decisions, or limitations that seemed insignificant when the report was written. At that point, the quality of the original documentation can become just as important as the forensic result itself. This session approaches forensic reporting from the perspective of the prosecutor who must ultimately present and defend that work in court. Attendees will examine the questions prosecutors should be asking forensic examiners before trial, the questions defense attorneys and experts are likely to ask on cross-examination, and the documentation practices that make forensic conclusions easier to explain and defend MVS Capture the Flag Another amazing Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag (CTF) is coming to Magnet Virtual Summit 2027! The CTF will be powered by Hexordia and it will be a three-hour timed event that will test your skills while competing with others. We don’t want to give away too much, but we promise that Jessica Hyde and interns from Champlain College’s Digital Forensic Association have created a CTF that will be fun, challenging, and full of learning opportunities. This CTF will take place on Thursday, February 11 from 11:00 – 2:00 PM ET and it will test your skills while competing with others. Important: Please note registration for this event closes at 4PM ET on February 8 and images and download links will be sent no later than February 9. Need a few tips on taking part in the competition? When you register, you can also sign up for a Capture the Flag workshop on February 8 at 12:00 PM ET with CTF creator, Jessica Hyde, and multiple Magnet CTF-winner, Kevin Pagano. Live Q&A with Magnet Forensics experts Drop into these live interactive sessions and chat directly with Magnet Forensics product experts. You’ll have the opportunity to engage in conversation with Product Management, Forensic Consulting, and Market Research team members from Magnet Forensics. And be sure to join us right before each Live Q&A for a special presentation that will cover the latest Magnet Forensics solutions. Learn more and register for Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 Get access to all these presentations, plus get opportunities to take part in special MVS games to gain points, and win prizes. Head over to www.magnetvirtualsummit.com for more information and to register and start building out your personalized agenda today.
