items.title: Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials From Infected Computers
items.summary: A Russian-speaking cybercrime operation has been stealing logins for US banks, the IRS and Social Security from infected Windows PCs. The victims were ordinary people. Many used a password manager and multi-factor authentication (MFA), and it did not help. The attackers did not break into any bank or government agency. They went after the victim’s own computer, where saved passwords, cookies and password vaults sit in one place. At least 57 US victims had a bank or government login in the stolen data. At least 46 had an ID.me, Login.gov, IRS or Social Security account. Researchers at Hunt.io found the operation through an exposed open directory on a server in the Netherlands. The folder held the attackers’ stolen data, scripts and logs, and it showed that 603 infected computers were reporting to the group’s servers. Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials The attackers began with a small Python file that runs quietly in the background on Windows. Hunt.io says it was delivered by phishing, though it did not give the exact lure. Once it was running, the infected PC checked in with the attackers’ servers, and they sent more tools based on what the victim had stored. The first target was the web browser. The attackers broke the encryption Chrome and Edge use to protect saved passwords. Their scripts carried built-in keys that unlocked the stolen browser files later, away from the victim’s PC. Hunt.io counted at least 3,345 decrypted logins from 16 victims, along with 30 cookie databases. Cookies matter because they prove a user has already signed in. When an attacker copies one, the website may treat the attacker as the real user. This is how session cookie theft leads to account takeovers even when MFA is turned on. Full infrastructure map (Source – Hunt.io) In this case the attackers replayed stolen Microsoft 365 cookies to get live access tokens without a password or MFA prompt. Password managers did not stop them either. One victim lost an entire LastPass vault with 2,880 logins, including Chase, Wells Fargo, IRS.gov, Medicare and PayPal. Criminals have long cracking weak master passwords offline in stolen vaults. Here the group instead decrypted the vault data straight from the victim’s browser files. They also guessed the master passwords of two 1Password users and copied a KeePass database from a developer’s computer. The stolen data pointed to major US banks. Chase appeared in 31 victims’ data, Capital One in 20, Citi in 17 and Wells Fargo in 15. The ID.me and Login.gov accounts are the most worrying part, because those services open the door to the IRS, Social Security and the VA. Wider Theft and the Attackers’ Hidden Setup The group did not stop at banks. Hunt.io found 6,570 cryptocurrency records from 67 victims, covering 44 platforms such as Binance, Coinbase, MetaMask and Kraken. The attackers also went after login tokens from 35 AI tools, including Claude, Codex and Gemini. These tokens can expose chat history, project files and API keys. To keep access after a cleanup, the attackers installed legitimate remote-management tools, Level.io and ScreenConnect. Because these are real business products, they can slip past some security filters. The setup was built to stay hidden. One server ran three control systems, named HavoX, Phantom53 and Kraken Bridge. Twelve Cloudflare Workers domains sat in front of them, so victim traffic looked like normal web traffic. Complete attack chain (Source – Hunt.io) Hunt.io says the system handled more than 1.2 million check-in messages over about three weeks. This kind of theft often ends in resale. Stolen logs can show up in an AI-powered marketplace selling infected computers. Hunt.io did not report a sale in this case. Its evidence of who is behind the operation is the Russian-language text in the attackers’ own files. It found that text across 249 scripts and logs. Home users who think a PC may be infected should use a clean device to change passwords, starting with email and banking. They should also sign out of every active session. Passwords alone are not enough, because a stolen session can stay valid after a reset. Security teams should watch for pythonw.exe running .pyw files from the AppData\Roaming folder, which is where these implants live. They should also block the listed domains and IPs. Hunt.io also advises binding sessions to compliant devices, keeping token lifetimes short and treating AI tool login files like SSH keys. items.title: CISA Warns Hackers Are Actively Exploiting Four Flaws in Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 18, 2026, after finding evidence that attackers were already exploiting them. The entries cover Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis and Vanderbilt University’s Research Electronic Data Capture platform, better known as REDCap. The four products serve different roles: network storage, access to AI models, legacy web services and research data collection. That makes this update relevant to more than one IT team. A storage administrator may own the Synology fix, but finding Apache Axis may require asking application vendors whether they bundle the library. CISA’s listing confirms exploitation of each flaw, not that the same attackers used all four. CISA noted evidence of active exploitation in its November 18 security alert, but the agency did not identify any malware in that notice. Separate reporting has linked attacks against Synology storage to C3RB3R ransomware and documented cryptomining malware in a REDCap incident. Those are incident-specific findings, not evidence of a shared campaign. Flaws in Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap CVE-2024-10441 is an output-handling flaw in a Synology system service that can let a remote attacker run code without signing in or requiring a user to take action. The original Synology vulnerability coverage lists fixed builds across several DSM branches, including 7.2.2-72806-1 and 7.2.1-69057-6. Those builds are historical patch thresholds; administrators should install the latest supported release for their device. CVE-2026-40217 affects LiteLLM’s custom guardrail testing feature. Guardrails are rules that control what an AI application accepts or returns. In this case, code meant to run inside a restricted test environment could escape those limits. The maintainers say the feature requires proxy administrator credentials in default configurations and recommend upgrading to version 1.83.11 or later. Earlier coverage of other LiteLLM gateway flaws explains why teams should also review what credentials and connected services the gateway can reach. CVE-2026-90436 affects Apache Axis 1.x, a discontinued Java library for SOAP web services. The flaw can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a vulnerable server. Rapid7 observed exploitation in a Confluence Data Center environment, where the attacker used the application’s credentials to access its database. Apache does not plan to ship a fixed Axis 1.x release. Organizations using software that bundles Axis should follow that product vendor’s guidance; for Confluence Data Center, that means upgrading to 9.2.28 or an unaffected 10.x release. CVE-2026-90817 is a code injection flaw in REDCap that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on the server. Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash, an identifier associated with a survey. That prerequisite does not make the issue harmless: teams running public surveys should confirm their REDCap version and prioritize the vendor’s remediation guidance. The survey hash is not a malware file hash or an indicator of compromise. Patch Deadlines and What Defenders Should Check Federal civilian agencies face a November 21 deadline for Synology DSM, Apache Axis and REDCap, and a December 2 deadline for LiteLLM. CISA’s directive also sets expectations for checking whether attackers compromised certain systems before they were patched. Recent coverage of an exploited Check Point flaw illustrates why that distinction matters: an update can close the entry point, but it cannot tell administrators what happened before installation. Start with internet-facing systems and confirm which versions are actually running. For storage appliances, review unexpected logins, new administrator accounts and unfamiliar scheduled tasks. Earlier reporting on Synology NAS ransomware attacks also recommends removing direct internet access to DSM management and keeping independent offline or off-site backups. Where Axis is embedded in another product, verify the fix against the host product’s version rather than assuming a separate Axis package will appear in inventory. items.title: Russian National Accused of Using Remote Access Tools to Spy on Silicon Valley Defense Firm
items.summary: A federal grand jury has indicted Russian national Igor D’iu over an alleged spy operation targeting employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. The U.S. Department of Justice said on Nov. 18 that D’iu bought remote access software and wireless networking equipment at the direction of people who recruited him through Telegram. Prosecutors say the group targeted the company because it supplied weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The department did not name the firm, which has an office in Palo Alto, California. According to the Justice Department’s announcement , D’iu’s alleged handlers told him to place his laptop near the company so they could connect to it remotely and try to gather information about employees nearby. They also allegedly directed him to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto office, identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens. The department published images it says D’iu took of employees’ computers. The department did not name the remote access software, say whether the handlers successfully connected to D’iu’s laptop, or report a breach of the company’s network. The device they allegedly wanted to control was D’iu’s own computer. That differs from other cases Cybersecurity News has covered, where attackers abused legitimate remote access tools to control victims’ computers . D’iu took of employees’ computers (Source: U.S. Department of Justice ) The alleged surveillance extended beyond the workplace. Investigators say D’iu searched for employees’ home addresses, including that of a senior executive. On Sept. 3, he allegedly followed an employee for nearly 30 miles as she drove from Palo Alto toward San Francisco. She called 911 and drove to a police station. Prosecutors say D’iu stopped following her after she contacted an officer. During searches in October, FBI agents recovered about $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, wireless networking gear, and false identity documents. They also found a notebook with 10 handwritten addresses, several of which matched employees’ homes. D’iu’s Russian passport (Source: U.S. Department of Justice ) Detailed profiles of at least three employees included relatives’ names, education and work histories, and notes on their strengths and weaknesses. Cybersecurity News previously reported on Russian military intelligence targeting Western logistics and technology firms . A joint advisory published by CISA and its partners described a separate cyber espionage campaign against organizations involved in getting aid to Ukraine. The Justice Department did not link D’iu to that campaign. The allegations against him show why defense firms should take reports of employees being followed or work screens being photographed seriously, even when there is no sign of a network breach. D’iu’s falsified American passport (Source : U.S. Department of Justice ) D’iu faces four charges: conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as a foreign agent without notifying the U.S. Attorney General, interstate stalking, and identification document fraud. He has been in federal custody since his Nov. 2 court appearance and is scheduled to return to court on Nov. 24. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. items.summary: .kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column491003_6bab7a-f6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Chrome 158 fixes 204 security issues, including six rated critical Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge used AI to find two critical flaws Update Chrome to get the security fixes, including on Android On November 17, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 158.0.8127.36/.37 for Windows and Mac, and 158.0.8127.36 for Linux . It includes 204 security fixes, six of which are rated critical—the highest severity level. Google also released Chrome 158.0.8127.42 for Android on November 17, with the same security fixes. It’s rolling out through Google Play . On November 18, Google released Chrome 159.0.8154.18 for Android to a small percentage of users. It will become available to more users over the next few days. Google credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge, assisted by Claude, with finding the critical GPU and Media flaws. Ge is also credited with finding several high-severity flaws. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can fall behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . Technical details The update addresses six vulnerabilities Google rates critical, all involving memory-safety errors. These include out-of-bounds writes in GPU and ANGLE, a buffer overflow in Media, and use-after-free vulnerabilities in WebView, GarbageCollection, and WebAudio. items.title: Hackers Exploit Microsoft 365 Device Code Authentication to Hijack Accounts and Bypass MFA
items.summary: Hackers are targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with fake payment notices and SharePoint documents that lead employees to a genuine Microsoft sign-in page. The November 2026 campaigns turn a routine task, such as checking whether an invoice was paid, into an authorization request that can give an attacker access to the employee’s account. The trick does not require breaking multifactor authentication (MFA) or stealing a password. As earlier coverage of Microsoft device code phishing showed, a real Microsoft sign-in page can still be part of a phishing attack. The employee may complete every security prompt correctly while unknowingly authorizing a session the attacker started. Researchers at Hornetsecurity’s Threat Intelligence Lab identified malicious HTML and SVG attachments in several payment-themed campaigns. The attachments redirected recipients or displayed phishing content; the report did not describe a separate malware implant. Researchers also did not name the operators or say how many accounts the campaigns compromised. Hackers Exploit Microsoft 365 Device Code Authentication In one case, the email’s subject was a single period, and the body offered almost no explanation. A personalized ZIP filename did the work of making the message look like payment advice. Inside was a file that appeared to be HTML but contained an interactive SVG, a type of image that can run scripts when opened as a browser document. What looked like a security check was actually a redirect. The redirect led to a counterfeit SharePoint workspace advertising remittance reports and check images. A second campaign used a scheduled electronic payment notice and a ZIP named SpwcinBillPaymentReports.zip . Device-code phishing workflow (Source – HornetSecurity) Its attachment rebuilt a document lure from hundreds of concealed fragments. Earlier reporting on browser-based phishing concealment illustrates why a static scan may miss what a recipient eventually sees, though it does not establish a link between the campaigns. Device code authentication is designed for devices such as shared displays that cannot easily handle a full sign-in. A user enters a short code on another device to authorize the original request. In these campaigns, the fake workspace supplied the code under the pretext of unlocking payment documents. When the employee signed in and completed any required MFA, Microsoft issued tokens to the client that initiated the request. That client belonged to the attacker. The tokens let the attacker act within the permissions granted to that client. Depending on those permissions, corporate email or files could be exposed. The FBI’s earlier Kali365 account hijacking warning documented the same authorization risk in a separate operation. Hornetsecurity also observed the fake workspace checking its session status, traffic that defenders can correlate with sign-in records. Detecting and Blocking Device Code Phishing Security teams should start with Microsoft Entra sign-in logs. Filter Authentication Protoco l for Device code , then check whether successful sign-ins match an expected application, account, source and time. The Original transfer method field can help trace sessions that began with device code authentication even if a later token renewal used another flow. Compare suspicious events with email, browser and network records. Microsoft’s Conditional Access configuration guide recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible. In Entra, select Authentication flows , choose Device code flow , and set the grant control to Block access . Start in Report-only mode to check which legitimate workflows would be affected. Keep exceptions narrow, document why each one is needed, and regularly review emergency-access exclusions before and after enforcement. A new policy is not a substitute for investigating an account that may already be compromised. If an employee entered an unsolicited code and finished signing in, revoke the account’s sign-in sessions and review subsequent activity for unauthorized access. As earlier coverage of OAuth device code abuse explains, email filtering and domain blocklists address only part of the problem. Employees should verify unexpected payment requests through a trusted channel and enter a device code only for a sign-in they started themselves. items.title: CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX2Root HTTP/2 Flaw Enables Remote Code Execution
items.summary: F5 has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-123007, a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in NGINX that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on vulnerable web servers. Dubbed NGINX2Root , the flaw resides in NGINX’s HTTP/2 flow-control implementation and has been present in the codebase for more than a decade. The vulnerability carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 . An attacker who can reach an HTTP/2-enabled NGINX listener can manipulate flow-control state until an invalid response length causes out-of-bounds memory access. Depending on the target environment, exploitation can crash an NGINX worker, disclose memory, corrupt process memory, or enable arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the worker process. NGINX Open Source releases from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 are vulnerable. F5 released fixed versions 1.30.7 for the stable branch and 1.31.9 for mainline on November 18, 2026. NGINX Plus is also affected across multiple 37.x and older supported branches. The flaw is particularly concerning because authentication is not required. Xint researchers demonstrated remote command execution through a reachable HTTP/2 service, while Rapid7 independently developed an unauthenticated RCE exploit against NGINX 1.31.8. However, obtaining root privileges on the underlying operating system requires a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability or another post-exploitation technique. Organizations can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, enabling security teams to operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, refine existing rules, and adapt behavioral detections to their organization’s telemetry. Contact Sales Detect CVE-2026-123007 by combining HTTP/2 network telemetry with NGINX worker behavior, crash events, and host-level process activity. Suspicious HTTP/2 traffic followed by worker segmentation faults, abnormal child processes, shell execution, or unexpected outbound connections from NGINX should receive immediate investigation. CVE-2026-123007 analysis CVE-2026-123007 affects NGINX deployments using HTTP/2. The vulnerability originates in the way NGINX manages HTTP/2 flow-control windows, which determine how much DATA a server can transmit to a client across individual streams and the overall connection. HTTP/2 clients can increase available flow-control credit using WINDOW_UPDATE frames. NGINX maintains separate counters for individual streams and the connection itself. The protocol limits these flow-control windows to 2^31-1 bytes, but the vulnerable implementation can be manipulated into exceeding the permitted connection-window threshold. Rapid7’s analysis describes a multi-stage condition in which an attacker keeps response data queued, manipulates stream and connection credits, and forces selected streams to close. Cleanup of those streams can restore reserved credit to the connection counter, pushing it above the HTTP/2 maximum. A subsequent unsigned subtraction can then underflow, allowing additional WINDOW_UPDATE frames to drive the counter to an invalid value. Eventually, NGINX interprets the excessive unsigned connection window as a negative signed response length. During buffered output processing, that value can be converted into an extremely large unsigned length passed to memory-copy operations, resulting in out-of-bounds reads and writes in the NGINX worker’s heap. The immediate result is often a worker segmentation fault. Under favorable memory-layout conditions, however, researchers demonstrated that the corruption can be converted into controlled memory disclosure and modification. This can ultimately provide arbitrary code execution within the NGINX worker process. F5 notes that code execution is possible when Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is disabled or when an attacker can bypass it. Wiz researchers reported successfully defeating ASLR in laboratory testing, while Xint demonstrated remote exploitation against publicly reachable servers. Execution initially occurs with the privileges assigned to the NGINX worker, rather than automatically providing root access. Xint separately identified a Linux kernel SCTP vulnerability that could be chained after NGINX compromise to escalate privileges and, in its demonstration, escape a Docker container and obtain root access to the underlying host. That kernel issue is separate from the NGINX vulnerability itself. The CVE-2026-123007 PoC situation substantially increases the urgency of remediation. Rapid7 publicly released exploit code demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 running in a Linux x86-64 Docker environment. Xint published demonstrations but intentionally omitted the final exploitation steps from its research. The currently public RCE technique is not equally reliable against every vulnerable server. Rapid7’s implementation requires approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic and depends on a specific x86-64 glibc memory-copy implementation selected on systems exposing AVX-512 features. In Rapid7’s test environment, exploitation took approximately two and a half minutes. Bandwidth and connection lifetime therefore affect practicality. Rapid7 estimates that transmitting the required traffic takes roughly two minutes over a 10 Gbit/s connection and around 17 minutes over 1 Gbit/s. Slower links can collide with NGINX’s default one-hour connection lifetime, while HTTP/2-terminating proxies may alter the frame sequence enough to prevent the demonstrated exploitation method from succeeding. These constraints should not be interpreted as making the vulnerability low risk. Multiple research teams independently achieved code execution, and alternative exploitation techniques could emerge now that the vulnerability and its underlying memory-corruption primitive are public. The flaw dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 , released on September 22, 2015, when HTTP/2 support first appeared. As a result, more than ten years of releases contain the vulnerable code. Xint reports discovering the issue on October 11, 2026 and submitting it to F5 through HackerOne on October 16. Coordinated public disclosure and patched NGINX releases followed on November 18. For CVE-2026-123007 detection, security teams should correlate abnormal HTTP/2 activity with NGINX error logs, service restarts, operating-system crash telemetry, and endpoint behavior. Repeated worker segmentation faults or unexplained NGINX worker exits occurring alongside unusual HTTP/2 connections should be treated as potential exploitation attempts. Post-exploitation monitoring is equally important. Defenders should investigate any NGINX worker process spawning shells or utilities such as sh, bash, curl, wget, Python interpreters, or other unexpected binaries. New outbound connections, file creation in unusual locations, privilege-escalation activity, or container escape behavior after suspicious HTTP/2 traffic should substantially increase alert severity. Traditional CVE-2026-123007 IOCs such as fixed malicious domains, hashes, or attacker IP addresses are currently limited because exploitation is protocol-driven and does not require a predefined payload infrastructure. Organizations should prioritize behavioral indicators and HTTP/2 exploitation patterns rather than relying solely on blocklists. As of November 19, 2026, neither F5 nor the reviewed security researchers have reported confirmed real-world exploitation, and the vulnerability has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Nevertheless, the availability of public exploit code significantly increases the likelihood of scanning and exploitation attempts against exposed systems. Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-123007 should review both F5’s security guidance and their operating-system or NGINX package vendor advisories because downstream distributions may backport fixes without matching upstream NGINX version numbers exactly. CVE-2026-123007 Mitigation The primary CVE-2026-123007 mitigation is to upgrade vulnerable NGINX installations immediately. The official NGINX security advisory lists the following Open Source ranges: Product Vulnerable versions Fixed version NGINX Open Source mainline 1.31.0–1.31.8 1.31.9 NGINX Open Source stable/older 1.9.5–1.30.6 1.30.7 NGINX Plus 37.1.0–37.2.0.1 37.3.0.1 NGINX Plus 7.0.0–37.0.7.1 37.0.8.1 NGINX Plus R34–R36 No fixed build listed in the reviewed advisory Organizations should prioritize internet-facing NGINX instances, reverse proxies, API gateways, web applications, Kubernetes ingress infrastructure, and other systems where HTTP/2 is exposed to untrusted clients. Administrators should also confirm whether HTTP/2 is actually enabled rather than relying only on package inventory. NGINX configurations can enable it through a listen directive containing http2 or, on newer releases, with http2 on;. An HTTP/2-capable listener negotiating the h2 ALPN protocol represents the relevant exposure path. Where an immediate upgrade is impossible, temporarily disabling HTTP/2 blocks the attack path for this vulnerability. Red Hat recommends removing the http2 parameter from affected listen directives and setting http2 off; on NGINX versions that support that directive. This workaround should be treated only as an interim measure. F5’s November 18 security release addresses multiple additional NGINX vulnerabilities, several of which do not depend on HTTP/2. Disabling HTTP/2 therefore does not replace installation of the updated packages. Administrators should also consider the operational impact before disabling HTTP/2. Applications that depend on native HTTP/2 functionality, including certain gRPC deployments, can stop functioning correctly when forced back to HTTP/1.1. After updating, organizations should ensure that the patched executable is actually running. A full service restart may be necessary rather than relying only on a configuration reload, particularly where older worker processes could remain active. Internet-facing systems that were vulnerable before remediation should be reviewed retrospectively. Security teams should examine NGINX error logs for worker crashes, operating-system logs for segmentation faults, network telemetry for unusually large or long-lived HTTP/2 sessions, and endpoint telemetry for suspicious execution originating from NGINX workers. Because public exploit code now exists, patching should be treated as an urgent exposure-reduction measure even though confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks has not yet been reported. FAQ What is CVE-2026-123007 and how does it work? CVE-2026-123007 is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in NGINX’s HTTP/2 flow-control implementation. A remote unauthenticated attacker can manipulate HTTP/2 window accounting until the connection’s flow-control value exceeds its permitted limit. The resulting integer underflow can cause NGINX to calculate an invalid response length, leading to out-of-bounds heap access. Successful exploitation can crash the worker or, under suitable conditions, enable arbitrary code execution. When was CVE-2026-123007 first discovered? Xint reports discovering the vulnerability on October 11, 2026 while conducting security research ahead of ZeroDay Cloud 2026. The researchers submitted the issue through HackerOne on October 16, completed patch validation with the NGINX team on November 10, and publicly disclosed the vulnerability alongside F5’s security updates on November 18, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-123007 on systems? Successful exploitation can cause denial of service through NGINX worker crashes, disclose or corrupt process memory, or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution with the privileges of the NGINX worker process. Root access is not an inherent result of the flaw, although researchers demonstrated chaining NGINX compromise with a separate Linux kernel vulnerability to obtain root privileges. Can CVE-2026-123007 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Any deployment running a vulnerable NGINX version with HTTP/2 enabled can remain exposed until it is updated or HTTP/2 is disabled. The vulnerable code spans Open Source releases from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, meaning both older installations and servers running recently released NGINX versions may require remediation. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123007? Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or install the corresponding fixed NGINX Plus release provided by F5. If immediate patching is impossible, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on vulnerable listeners and restrict unnecessary public exposure. After remediation, restart affected NGINX services and review historical telemetry for worker crashes, suspicious HTTP/2 activity, and unexpected process execution originating from NGINX.

These constraints should not be interpreted as making the vulnerability low risk. Multiple research teams independently achieved code execution, and alternative exploitation techniques could emerge now that the vulnerability and its underlying memory-corruption primitive are public.

The flaw dates back to NGINX 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015, when HTTP/2 support first appeared. As a result, more than ten years of releases contain the vulnerable code. Xint reports discovering the issue on October 11, 2026 and submitting it to F5 through HackerOne on October 16. Coordinated public disclosure and patched NGINX releases followed on November 18.

For CVE-2026-123007 detection, security teams should correlate abnormal HTTP/2 activity with NGINX error logs, service restarts, operating-system crash telemetry, and endpoint behavior. Repeated worker segmentation faults or unexplained NGINX worker exits occurring alongside unusual HTTP/2 connections should be treated as potential exploitation attempts.

Post-exploitation monitoring is equally important. Defenders should investigate any NGINX worker process spawning shells or utilities such as sh, bash, curl, wget, Python interpreters, or other unexpected binaries. New outbound connections, file creation in unusual locations, privilege-escalation activity, or container escape behavior after suspicious HTTP/2 traffic should substantially increase alert severity.

Traditional CVE-2026-123007 IOCs such as fixed malicious domains, hashes, or attacker IP addresses are currently limited because exploitation is protocol-driven and does not require a predefined payload infrastructure. Organizations should prioritize behavioral indicators and HTTP/2 exploitation patterns rather than relying solely on blocklists.

As of November 19, 2026, neither F5 nor the reviewed security researchers have reported confirmed real-world exploitation, and the vulnerability has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Nevertheless, the availability of public exploit code significantly increases the likelihood of scanning and exploitation attempts against exposed systems.

Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-123007 should review both F5’s security guidance and their operating-system or NGINX package vendor advisories because downstream distributions may backport fixes without matching upstream NGINX version numbers exactly.

CVE-2026-123007 Mitigation

The primary CVE-2026-123007 mitigation is to upgrade vulnerable NGINX installations immediately. The official NGINX security advisory lists the following Open Source ranges:

ProductVulnerable versionsFixed versionNGINX Open Source mainline1.31.0–1.31.81.31.9NGINX Open Source stable/older1.9.5–1.30.61.30.7NGINX Plus37.1.0–37.2.0.137.3.0.1NGINX Plus7.0.0–37.0.7.137.0.8.1NGINX PlusR34–R36No fixed build listed in the reviewed advisory

Organizations should prioritize internet-facing NGINX instances, reverse proxies, API gateways, web applications, Kubernetes ingress infrastructure, and other systems where HTTP/2 is exposed to untrusted clients.

Administrators should also confirm whether HTTP/2 is actually enabled rather than relying only on package inventory. NGINX configurations can enable it through a listen directive containing http2 or, on newer releases, with http2 on;. An HTTP/2-capable listener negotiating the h2 ALPN protocol represents the relevant exposure path.

Where an immediate upgrade is impossible, temporarily disabling HTTP/2 blocks the attack path for this vulnerability. Red Hat recommends removing the http2 parameter from affected listen directives and setting http2 off; on NGINX versions that support that directive.

This workaround should be treated only as an interim measure. F5’s November 18 security release addresses multiple additional NGINX vulnerabilities, several of which do not depend on HTTP/2. Disabling HTTP/2 therefore does not replace installation of the updated packages.

Administrators should also consider the operational impact before disabling HTTP/2. Applications that depend on native HTTP/2 functionality, including certain gRPC deployments, can stop functioning correctly when forced back to HTTP/1.1.

After updating, organizations should ensure that the patched executable is actually running. A full service restart may be necessary rather than relying only on a configuration reload, particularly where older worker processes could remain active.

Internet-facing systems that were vulnerable before remediation should be reviewed retrospectively. Security teams should examine NGINX error logs for worker crashes, operating-system logs for segmentation faults, network telemetry for unusually large or long-lived HTTP/2 sessions, and endpoint telemetry for suspicious execution originating from NGINX workers.

Because public exploit code now exists, patching should be treated as an urgent exposure-reduction measure even though confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks has not yet been reported.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-123007 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-123007 is a critical memory-corruption vulnerability in NGINX’s HTTP/2 flow-control implementation. A remote unauthenticated attacker can manipulate HTTP/2 window accounting until the connection’s flow-control value exceeds its permitted limit. The resulting integer underflow can cause NGINX to calculate an invalid response length, leading to out-of-bounds heap access. Successful exploitation can crash the worker or, under suitable conditions, enable arbitrary code execution.

When was CVE-2026-123007 first discovered?

Xint reports discovering the vulnerability on October 11, 2026 while conducting security research ahead of ZeroDay Cloud 2026. The researchers submitted the issue through HackerOne on October 16, completed patch validation with the NGINX team on November 10, and publicly disclosed the vulnerability alongside F5’s security updates on November 18, 2026.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-123007 on systems?

Successful exploitation can cause denial of service through NGINX worker crashes, disclose or corrupt process memory, or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution with the privileges of the NGINX worker process. Root access is not an inherent result of the flaw, although researchers demonstrated chaining NGINX compromise with a separate Linux kernel vulnerability to obtain root privileges.

Can CVE-2026-123007 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Any deployment running a vulnerable NGINX version with HTTP/2 enabled can remain exposed until it is updated or HTTP/2 is disabled. The vulnerable code spans Open Source releases from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, meaning both older installations and servers running recently released NGINX versions may require remediation.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123007?

Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or install the corresponding fixed NGINX Plus release provided by F5. If immediate patching is impossible, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on vulnerable listeners and restrict unnecessary public exposure. After remediation, restart affected NGINX services and review historical telemetry for worker crashes, suspicious HTTP/2 activity, and unexpected process execution originating from NGINX.

items.title: CVE-2026-123633: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free Flaw Enables RCE
items.summary: A newly disclosed vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-123633 exposes certain NGINX reverse-proxy deployments to unauthenticated denial-of-service attacks and potentially remote code execution. The flaw is a use-after-free condition in NGINX’s HTTP/2 processing that can be triggered when the server proxies client requests to an upstream backend while a worker is running low on available connections. The vulnerability was disclosed alongside CVE-2026-123007 as part of a broader set of security flaws patched by the NGINX team on November 18, 2026. F5 assigns CVE-2026-123633 a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, Critical , while its CVSS v3.1 score is 8.1, High because exploitation requires a particular server state and configuration. Unlike CVE-2026-123007, which can affect HTTP/2-enabled NGINX instances serving ordinary static content, CVE-2026-123633 specifically targets reverse-proxy processing. An exposed server must have HTTP/2 enabled, forward requests to a backend server, and reach a state where available worker_connections are running low. Successful exploitation can crash NGINX worker processes or corrupt memory. Wiz researchers demonstrated that the vulnerability can be developed into unauthenticated remote code execution and confirmed an ASLR bypass in laboratory environments. Code execution occurs with the privileges of the NGINX worker process rather than automatically granting root access to the host. Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Contact Sales Detect CVE-2026-123633 by correlating abnormal HTTP/2 traffic and connection exhaustion with NGINX worker crashes, suspicious process execution, and unexpected network connections originating from NGINX processes. Because exploitation occurs in the web-server process itself, combining network and endpoint telemetry provides substantially stronger visibility than relying on static indicators alone. CVE-2026-123633 analysis CVE-2026-123633 affects NGINX Open Source versions beginning with 1.19.7 through 1.31.8 when HTTP/2 is enabled and requests are proxied to an upstream backend. NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 contain the fix. NGINX Plus is also affected, with fixes for this specific vulnerability introduced in 37.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1. The underlying weakness is a use-after-free condition in NGINX’s HTTP/2 connection management. NGINX keeps a list of connections marked as reusable so it can close them when additional connection slots are required. A connection should only remain on that list when it has no active request being processed. Researchers found that an attacker can initially send only part of an HTTP/2 HEADERS frame. Because no active stream has yet been created, NGINX marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the remainder of the frame. After the attacker sends the remaining portion, NGINX creates an HTTP/2 request stream and begins processing the request. However, the connection can incorrectly remain marked as reusable even though it is now actively handling a request. This creates the precondition for the memory-safety flaw. The attacker then causes the request to be forwarded to an upstream application server. Establishing that backend connection requires NGINX to obtain another connection slot. When the worker approaches its configured worker_connections limit, NGINX can invoke its connection-draining logic to free capacity. Because the malicious HTTP/2 connection was incorrectly left on the reusable list, NGINX can select and close that same connection even while its request is still being processed. During connection cleanup, memory associated with the HTTP/2 connection can be freed while other portions of the request-processing path still retain references to it. Execution subsequently continues through those stale pointers, producing a classic use-after-free condition. If the freed memory is reallocated for attacker-influenced data, the NGINX worker can interpret new contents as the original HTTP/2 request or connection structures. This memory corruption can initially cause a segmentation fault or worker crash. More advanced exploitation requires manipulating memory allocation so that attacker-controlled data occupies the freed region. Researchers showed that the primitive can be extended to disclose memory addresses, manipulate heap state, defeat ASLR, and ultimately achieve arbitrary code execution. F5’s vulnerability description states that code execution is possible when ASLR is disabled or when an attacker can bypass it. Wiz researchers went further and reported successfully developing an ASLR bypass, demonstrating that ASLR should not be considered a sufficient protection against a determined attacker. The attack is remote and does not require authentication. However, exploitation has several environmental prerequisites: the attacker must communicate directly with an HTTP/2-enabled NGINX listener, that instance must proxy requests to a backend, and the targeted worker must reach a state where free connection slots are scarce. This makes the flaw particularly relevant to heavily utilized reverse proxies, API gateways, ingress infrastructure, SaaS front ends, and web platforms where NGINX handles large numbers of concurrent HTTP/2 connections while forwarding traffic to application servers. A CDN or WAF that terminates HTTP/2 before traffic reaches the NGINX origin may disrupt the precise frame behavior required for exploitation. However, researchers caution that protection depends on the intermediary’s implementation and should not be treated as a substitute for updating the underlying NGINX instance. The CVE-2026-123633 PoC status requires some nuance. Wiz and Xint developed working exploitation techniques and demonstrated remote code execution during coordinated research, but Wiz explicitly stated that it would not release its full exploit. Several GitHub repositories claiming proof-of-concept implementations appeared after disclosure, but their existence should not be interpreted as independent validation of a reliable universal RCE exploit. Xint reports that its researchers discovered the group of NGINX vulnerabilities on October 11, 2026 and submitted them to F5 through HackerOne on October 16. F5 provided a patch for validation on November 10, followed by coordinated public disclosure on November 18. The vulnerability had been present since NGINX 1.19.7, meaning the affected code path remained in production releases for nearly six years before disclosure. A log entry indicating an NGINX worker exited on a signal can provide evidence of a failed exploitation attempt, although worker crashes alone are not high-confidence proof of malicious activity. Endpoint telemetry becomes especially important for detecting successful exploitation. NGINX worker processes unexpectedly launching sh, bash, curl, wget, Python, Perl, or other command interpreters should be treated as highly suspicious. Defenders should also investigate new outbound network connections, file downloads, persistence activity, or credential access initiated by NGINX worker processes. Network teams should monitor scenarios where one or more sources maintain large numbers of HTTP/2 connections while the affected server simultaneously experiences connection pressure or unexpected worker failures. Because the use-after-free depends on connection-draining behavior, this correlation may provide greater fidelity than simply alerting on high HTTP/2 volume. Traditional CVE-2026-123633 IOCs such as malware hashes, fixed attacker domains, or known command-and-control servers are currently of limited value. The vulnerability can be exploited directly over HTTP/2 without requiring a predefined malware payload or attacker-controlled infrastructure, making behavior-based monitoring and exposure management more effective. Nevertheless, working private exploits, detailed technical research, and public interest in the flaw make rapid remediation advisable. Confirm whether HTTP/2 is accepted on the origin, whether NGINX proxies those requests to upstream servers, and whether a CDN or another proxy terminates HTTP/2 before the traffic reaches NGINX. Moving to the latest vendor-recommended security build therefore provides broader protection against the vulnerabilities disclosed in the November security release. After installing an updated package, administrators should ensure the new binary is actually running. The Hacker News notes that a normal configuration reload may leave existing workers running the previous executable. Perform a full restart or appropriate live binary upgrade and confirm that old worker processes have exited. Organizations should test application compatibility before disabling HTTP/2 because native gRPC and other services can depend on HTTP/2 functionality. The workaround should therefore be treated as temporary rather than a permanent replacement for the security update. Administrators should inventory NGINX deployments acting as reverse proxies, ingress controllers, API gateways, or application front ends. Prioritize internet-facing instances that expose HTTP/2 and forward traffic to upstream application servers, since this combination provides the primary vulnerable configuration. Teams should also examine the worker_connections configuration and historical utilization. Raising the limit may make the specific exploitation condition more difficult to trigger, but it does not correct the underlying use-after-free and should not be treated as a security fix. Subsequent request processing then accesses the freed memory, potentially causing a crash, memory corruption, or remote code execution. When was CVE-2026-123633 first discovered? items.title: CVE-2026-129448: Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw Exploited in the Wild
items.summary: Apache has disclosed a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Apache Roller, an open-source Java-based blogging and content management platform. Tracked as CVE-2026-129448, the flaw enables an unauthenticated remote attacker to send malicious data to Roller’s XML-RPC endpoint and trigger deserialization before authentication checks occur. Apache has confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in real-world attacks. The vulnerability carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical , with low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. Successful exploitation can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the context of the application server, potentially providing control over the Roller deployment and access to data, credentials, or other resources available to the compromised Java process. Organizations that cannot upgrade immediately have two vendor-recommended temporary options. Administrators can set: enabledForExtensions=false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or completely remove the servlet mapping for: /roller-services/xmlrpc After making either change, Roller must be restarted for the mitigation to take effect. On vulnerable builds, the XML-RPC request body can already have been parsed and deserialized before the setting is evaluated. Organizations that do not require XML-RPC should consider removing or blocking access to the endpoint altogether in addition to upgrading. Restricting access at a reverse proxy or firewall can further reduce exposure, although network filtering should not replace the vendor update. Because exploitation is already occurring, organizations should treat vulnerable internet-facing Roller servers as potentially compromised. After upgrading, administrators should review web access logs, application logs, Java process telemetry, authentication records, file modifications, and outbound network activity dating back to the period before remediation. If suspicious process execution or other post-exploitation evidence is discovered, rotating credentials available to Roller should be part of incident response. This can include database credentials, application secrets, service credentials, API keys, and any authentication material accessible to the Java application server. The endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes attacker-controlled content while parsing the request, before authenticating the sender. An attacker can therefore trigger unsafe Java deserialization remotely and potentially execute arbitrary code on the affected server. When was CVE-2026-129448 first discovered? The exact private discovery date has not been publicly disclosed. The underlying vulnerability was initially addressed through work submitted to Apache Roller in late August and merged on September 5, 2026. It was first publicly disclosed under CVE-2026-82384 in late September for Roller 6.1.5. Apache later published CVE-2026-129448 on November 17, 2026 after determining that Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 were also affected. Security researcher n0mi1k is credited with finding the vulnerability, while Matt Raible is credited with reporting the broader issue. What is the impact of CVE-2026-129448 on systems? Successful exploitation can enable unauthenticated arbitrary code execution within the Java application server hosting Apache Roller. Depending on the privileges and configuration of that process, attackers could potentially access sensitive application data, retrieve credentials, modify files, establish persistence, disrupt service availability, or use the compromised server for further intrusion activity. Apache rates the flaw Critical with a CVSS score of 9.8. Can CVE-2026-129448 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Any organization still operating Apache Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 remains vulnerable to this CVE. Roller 6.1.5 is also vulnerable to the same underlying issue under CVE-2026-82384. Apache has confirmed active exploitation, so exposed systems should be considered high priority for remediation and compromise assessment. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-129448? Upgrade Apache Roller to 6.1.6 or later, preferably the latest supported release. If an immediate upgrade is impossible, disable vendor extension types in WEB-INF/web.xml or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping and restart Roller. Do not rely solely on disabling XML-RPC through the administrative interface. Because exploitation is already occurring, organizations should also inspect previously exposed systems for evidence of compromise.
items.summary_html:
Apache has disclosed a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Apache Roller, an open-source Java-based blogging and content management platform. Tracked as CVE-2026-129448, the flaw enables an unauthenticated remote attacker to send malicious data to Roller’s XML-RPC endpoint and trigger deserialization before authentication checks occur. Apache has confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in real-world attacks.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical, with low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. Successful exploitation can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the context of the application server, potentially providing control over the Roller deployment and access to data, credentials, or other resources available to the compromised Java process.

The issue affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It is the same underlying security weakness as CVE-2026-82384, which was disclosed in September 2026 and specifically documented Apache Roller 6.1.5 as vulnerable. Taken together, the two CVE records show that installations from Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.5 should be treated as vulnerable and upgraded to 6.1.6 or later.

The risk is heightened by the fact that disabling XML-RPC through the Roller administration interface alone does not prevent exploitation on vulnerable releases. The affected endpoint can deserialize attacker-controlled request content before the application checks whether XML-RPC functionality has been disabled.

Organizations can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence, accelerate threat hunting, and apply relevant detection logic across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Security teams can also use Prime Architect to turn emerging vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries, refine detection rules, and adapt behavioral detection logic to the telemetry available across their infrastructure.

CVE-2026-129448 analysis

CVE-2026-129448 affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. Apache describes the issue as Deserialization of Untrusted Data, mapped to CWE-502, in Roller’s XML-RPC functionality. The endpoint accepts non-standard vendor extension types and processes them before authenticating the client.

Apache Roller exposes an XML-RPC servlet at:

/roller-services/xmlrpc

The XML-RPC implementation historically allowed vendor-specific extension types in addition to standard XML-RPC values. Roller itself does not require those extension types, but older configurations enabled them at the servlet level.

The critical security issue is the order in which incoming requests are processed. The XML-RPC parser accepts and deserializes extension-type values while parsing the request body. Authentication and feature-state checks happen later. As a result, an unauthenticated attacker can cause attacker-controlled serialized data to reach Java deserialization logic before Roller has established whether the request should be permitted.

This ordering effectively places a dangerous deserialization primitive on a remotely reachable endpoint. In vulnerable deployments, an attacker does not need a valid Roller account, administrator credentials, or user interaction to reach the affected code path.

The original issue was first publicly documented under CVE-2026-82384 in September 2026. That advisory listed Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected and explained that the XML-RPC servlet is mapped unconditionally, meaning requests can still reach parsing logic even when administrators believe XML-RPC has been disabled through Roller’s configuration interface.

Further investigation later determined that older Roller releases were also vulnerable. Apache therefore published CVE-2026-129448 on November 17, 2026 to cover versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and explicitly confirmed that the issue was being exploited in the wild.

Apache has not disclosed who is exploiting the flaw, how many systems have been compromised, what organizations are being targeted, or which post-exploitation payloads have been observed. This means defenders should avoid assuming the threat is tied to a single campaign or malware family.

The flaw receives a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 with the vector:

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

This reflects network-based exploitation, low attack complexity, no authentication requirement, no user interaction, and potentially high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Successful exploitation can execute arbitrary code within the Java application server process hosting Roller. The exact privileges depend on how the application server, such as Apache Tomcat, is configured. An attacker gaining code execution could potentially access Roller configuration data, interact with the local filesystem, retrieve database credentials available to the application, establish persistence, or use the compromised host as a foothold for further activity.

The CVE-2026-129448 PoC landscape has also changed rapidly following disclosure. On November 19, public vulnerability indexes began tracking at least one exploit repository claiming to demonstrate exploitation of the XML-RPC deserialization path. Public exploit availability should increase the urgency of remediation, although defenders should distinguish between the existence of exploit code and Apache’s separate confirmation of real-world exploitation, which predates the public repository.

The issue is particularly dangerous because turning XML-RPC off in Roller’s administrative interface is insufficient on vulnerable releases. The server can parse the request and deserialize extension content before checking the global XML-RPC configuration flag. Apache therefore specifically warns administrators not to rely on the UI setting as a security control.

The patch implemented for Roller 6.1.6 changes this behavior in two important ways. First, vendor extension types are disabled because Roller only requires standard XML-RPC values. Second, the endpoint is gated earlier so that when XML-RPC is disabled, requests are rejected before their bodies are processed.

For CVE-2026-129448 detection, defenders should prioritize web server, application server, Java process, and network telemetry associated with Roller deployments. Requests to /roller-services/xmlrpc deserve particular attention, especially on systems where the organization does not intentionally use XML-RPC functionality.

Security teams should investigate unusual POST requests containing unexpected XML-RPC extension-type data, repeated requests from unfamiliar external sources, or attempts to interact with the endpoint despite XML-RPC being disabled operationally.

Endpoint telemetry can provide stronger evidence of successful exploitation. Java application server processes such as Tomcat unexpectedly spawning sh, bash, cmd.exe, PowerShell, curl, wget, Python, or other command interpreters should be treated as high-severity events.

Unexpected outbound network connections originating from the Roller or Tomcat process can also indicate post-exploitation activity. Defenders should correlate these events with inbound XML-RPC traffic and changes to files, scheduled jobs, service definitions, application directories, or startup configurations.

Traditional CVE-2026-129448 IOCs remain limited because Apache has not published attacker IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or campaign-specific infrastructure associated with the confirmed exploitation. Behavioral detection and review of Roller XML-RPC activity are therefore more reliable than static blocklists at this stage.

Organizations running vulnerable Roller instances should also consider retrospective investigation. Because Apache has confirmed exploitation without disclosing the time window or attack details, patching a system does not establish that the host was not compromised before remediation.

Security teams seeking additional details for CVE-2026-129448 should account for the relationship with CVE-2026-82384. The newer CVE covers Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, while the earlier advisory separately lists version 6.1.5 as vulnerable. Apache’s remediation guidance for both issues converges on Roller 6.1.6 or later.

CVE-2026-129448 Mitigation

The primary CVE-2026-129448 mitigation is to upgrade Apache Roller immediately. Apache recommends version 6.1.6 or later, while Roller 6.1.7 is currently listed by the project as the best available GA release.

The relevant exposure can be summarized as follows:

Organizations that cannot upgrade immediately have two vendor-recommended temporary options. Administrators can set:

enabledForExtensions=false

in WEB-INF/web.xml, or completely remove the servlet mapping for:

/roller-services/xmlrpc

After making either change, Roller must be restarted for the mitigation to take effect.

Simply disabling XML-RPC from the administration interface is not sufficient. On vulnerable builds, the XML-RPC request body can already have been parsed and deserialized before the setting is evaluated.

Organizations that do not require XML-RPC should consider removing or blocking access to the endpoint altogether in addition to upgrading. Restricting access at a reverse proxy or firewall can further reduce exposure, although network filtering should not replace the vendor update.

Because exploitation is already occurring, organizations should treat vulnerable internet-facing Roller servers as potentially compromised. After upgrading, administrators should review web access logs, application logs, Java process telemetry, authentication records, file modifications, and outbound network activity dating back to the period before remediation.

If suspicious process execution or other post-exploitation evidence is discovered, rotating credentials available to Roller should be part of incident response. This can include database credentials, application secrets, service credentials, API keys, and any authentication material accessible to the Java application server.

Security teams should also review whether the Roller service account has excessive operating-system permissions. Running the application with a dedicated low-privilege account reduces the potential impact of application-level code execution.

items.summary: A quick one with a fix for decoded patterns, and two for the Swift bindings. Patterns When decoding memory against a pattern, a field whose size can’t be worked out, because something inside it runs past the data, had none of its attributes applied. That is right for the ones that need the field’s value, but it also dropped the ones that only say how to present it: inline , hidden , sealed , name , comment and color . A view would thus draw a row for a member the author asked to have folded into its parent. Those are now kept. Swift A getter for a borrowed object made a new wrapper on every access. For an object that emits signals, that is a new event stream each time, and one that ends as soon as the wrapper goes away: taking device.bus.events and then calling device.bus.attach() never saw a message. Such a child is now stored once, as the hand-written bindings used to do for Device.bus . On Linux, a JSON number that happened to be 0 or 1 went out as false or true on its way through our marshaling. Foundation there casts such an NSNumber to Bool just as Darwin does, and we told the two apart by a CoreFoundation type that Linux does not show. A boolean is now told by its class, which is the same on both. Enjoy! Changelog patterns: Keep the presentation attributes of a field cut short by the end of the data. swift: Keep one wrapper for a child that emits signals, fixing lost events on e.g. device.bus . swift: Tell a JSON number from a boolean on Linux.
items.summary_html:
A quick one with a fix for decoded patterns, and two for the Swift bindings.

Patterns

When decoding memory against a pattern, a field whose size can’t be worked out, because something inside it runs past the data, had none of its attributes applied. That is right for the ones that need the field’s value, but it also dropped the ones that only say how to present it: inline, hidden, sealed, name, comment and color. A view would thus draw a row for a member the author asked to have folded into its parent. Those are now kept.

Swift

A getter for a borrowed object made a new wrapper on every access. For an object that emits signals, that is a new event stream each time, and one that ends as soon as the wrapper goes away: taking device.bus.events and then calling device.bus.attach() never saw a message. Such a child is now stored once, as the hand-written bindings used to do for Device.bus.

On Linux, a JSON number that happened to be 0 or 1 went out as false or true on its way through our marshaling. Foundation there casts such an NSNumber to Bool just as Darwin does, and we told the two apart by a CoreFoundation type that Linux does not show. A boolean is now told by its class, which is the same on both.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • patterns: Keep the presentation attributes of a field cut short by the end of the data.
  • swift: Keep one wrapper for a child that emits signals, fixing lost events on e.g. device.bus.
  • swift: Tell a JSON number from a boolean on Linux.

items.title: Scattered Spider’s phishing and SIM-swap tactics led to six-year sentence
items.summary: .kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column490927_e74642-57{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column490927_e74642-57 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Scattered Spider used phishing texts and SIM swaps to steal $11.6 million in cryptocurrency Tyler Robert Buchanan’s six-year sentence doesn’t mean the wider group has disappeared Follow our advice to protect your phone number and accounts from SIM swapping A US court has sentenced a member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group to six years in prison. Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man, joins four other group members in jail for his part in crimes that netted $11.6 million in proceeds. Texts, SIM swaps and $11.6 million Buchanan and his co-conspirators hacked at least a dozen companies in a years-long campaign, according to the Department of Justice. They sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages, also known as smishing , to employees at their target companies. The messages pretended to come from the employer or one of its contractors, such as an IT support provider. They contained links to phishing websites impersonating company websites and designed to steal usernames and passwords. The criminal group used those stolen credentials to access company systems. The group also used SIM swapping to steal from individuals. In a SIM swap, a criminal tricks a mobile phone carrier into transferring a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. The criminal can then receive calls and text messages intended for the victim, including SMS authentication codes. SIM swapping allowed Buchanan and his co-conspirators to take over cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing over $11.6 million from victims. Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and taken into US custody in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He faced a maximum possible sentence of 22 years. The other four defendants in the US case have also been sentenced. The longest sentence, 10 years, went to 22-year-old Floridian Noah Michael Urban, who pleaded guilty to fraud-related charges. Joel Martin Evans , aged 27, of North Carolina, is now serving a two-year federal prison sentence for conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both from Texas, each received 45-month sentences for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. Does this end the reign of Scattered Spider? Experts say it’s unlikely, partly because the group is fragmented. Cybersecurity company Group-IB has warned that it contains different subclusters connected by shared tools and techniques. Members sometimes share online chats, too, but the subclusters act separately and rarely include more than five people, the company said. There is also a significant overlap between Scattered Spider and an online group known as The Com, Group-IB said. The Com has been linked to child sexual abuse material and attacks on companies, including Allianz Life. Other Scattered Spider members were also sentenced in the UK in July this year. Eighteen-year-old Owen Flowers and 19-year-old Thalha Jubair each received five-and-a-half-year sentences for a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL). The youths live-streamed that attack in August 2024, which stole the personal data of up to 10 million TfL customers. We also reported last month on the arrest of another person linked to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The name brings together three groups—Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters—that have reportedly worked together on and off since summer 2025. How to protect your number from SIM swapping Phishing texts and SIM swaps can put both work systems and personal accounts at risk. These steps can make it harder for someone to take over your number or use it to access your accounts: Ask your mobile carrier whether it offers an account PIN, port-out lock, or number-transfer protection. These can make it harder for someone to move your number to another SIM. Where possible, use an authenticator app, passkey, or security key instead of SMS codes. In this article
  • Scattered Spider used phishing texts and SIM swaps to steal $11.6 million in cryptocurrency
  • Tyler Robert Buchanan’s six-year sentence doesn’t mean the wider group has disappeared
  • Follow our advice to protect your phone number and accounts from SIM swapping

A US court has sentenced a member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group to six years in prison. Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man, joins four other group members in jail for his part in crimes that netted $11.6 million in proceeds.

Texts, SIM swaps and $11.6 million

Buchanan and his co-conspirators hacked at least a dozen companies in a years-long campaign, according to the Department of Justice. They sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages, also known as smishing, to employees at their target companies. The messages pretended to come from the employer or one of its contractors, such as an IT support provider. They contained links to phishing websites impersonating company websites and designed to steal usernames and passwords. The criminal group used those stolen credentials to access company systems.

The group also used SIM swapping to steal from individuals. In a SIM swap, a criminal tricks a mobile phone carrier into transferring a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. The criminal can then receive calls and text messages intended for the victim, including SMS authentication codes.

SIM swapping allowed Buchanan and his co-conspirators to take over cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing over $11.6 million from victims.

Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and taken into US custody in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He faced a maximum possible sentence of 22 years.

The other four defendants in the US case have also been sentenced. The longest sentence, 10 years, went to 22-year-old Floridian Noah Michael Urban, who pleaded guilty to fraud-related charges.

Joel Martin Evans , aged 27, of North Carolina, is now serving a two-year federal prison sentence for conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both from Texas, each received 45-month sentences for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Does this end the reign of Scattered Spider?

Experts say it’s unlikely, partly because the group is fragmented. Cybersecurity company Group-IB has warned that it contains different subclusters connected by shared tools and techniques. Members sometimes share online chats, too, but the subclusters act separately and rarely include more than five people, the company said.

There is also a significant overlap between Scattered Spider and an online group known as The Com, Group-IB said. The Com has been linked to child sexual abuse material and attacks on companies, including Allianz Life.

Other Scattered Spider members were also sentenced in the UK in July this year. Eighteen-year-old Owen Flowers and 19-year-old Thalha Jubair each received five-and-a-half-year sentences for a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL). The youths live-streamed that attack in August 2024, which stole the personal data of up to 10 million TfL customers.

We also reported last month on the arrest of another person linked to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The name brings together three groups—Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters—that have reportedly worked together on and off since summer 2025.

How to protect your number from SIM swapping

Phishing texts and SIM swaps can put both work systems and personal accounts at risk. These steps can make it harder for someone to take over your number or use it to access your accounts:

  • Ask your mobile carrier whether it offers an account PIN, port-out lock, or number-transfer protection. These can make it harder for someone to move your number to another SIM.
  • Where possible, use an authenticator app, passkey, or security key instead of SMS codes. These options aren’t tied to your phone number in the same way.
  • Never approve a sign-in prompt you didn’t initiate. Attackers may flood you with requests in the hope that you’ll approve one.

Scammers know more about you than you think.
