items.title: Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 CTF: New challenges, new leaderboards
items.summary: Key takeaways Put your digital forensics skills to the test: Compete in a three-hour Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag featuring new forensic datasets, realistic investigative scenarios, and challenges for all experience levels. Choose how you compete: Join the Unassisted or AI-Assisted Leaderboard for a chance to win prizes, with additional cipher challenges offering an early opportunity to earn points. Get ready for the challenge: Join a virtual preparation workshop on February 8, download the forensic images in advance, and compete live on February 11. By Jessica Hyde, Founder & Owner of Hexordia I am thrilled to announce the launch of the Magnet Virtual Summit Capture the Flag (CTF), proudly sponsored by Hexordia ! This competition is a fun, interactive way to put your digital forensics skills to the test. Participants will work with forensic images from multiple simulated pieces of evidence and answer a variety of challenge questions based on the data. You are welcome to use any tools you prefer to solve the questions, which are assigned point values reflecting their complexity. The challenges are thoughtfully designed to accommodate all levels of expertise, from beginners to seasoned practitioners. We are incredibly enthusiastic about the entirely new data sets and questions we are preparing, and we eagerly await your participation! It has been an absolute pleasure collaborating with our exceptional group of interns, Matteen Mahfooz and Alex Vejandla from George Mason University, and our Hexordia team member, Adam Hachem. Furthermore, we are delighted that multi-CTF champion Kevin Pagano has also returned to join the team to construct this year’s competition. New leaderboard structure & prizes With this year’s CTF, we are introducing a brand-new leaderboard structure. The Magnet Virtual Summit CTF aims to replicate real-life scenarios in digital forensics and the use of artificial intelligence will be permitted, as it’s becoming an increasingly prevalent tool in investigations. Before starting the competition, please choose whether you will be competing on the Unassisted Leaderboard or the AI-Assisted Leaderboard. The AI-Assisted Leaderboard is available for participants using AI tools during the three-hour competition window only. Unassisted Leaderboard: First place, second place, and third place prizes AI-Assisted Leaderboard: First place prize Returning for the 2027 challenge: Cipher questions Back by popular demand for the 2027 challenge, keep a close watch on our social media channels in the weeks leading up to the main event! We will once again be releasing a series of intriguing cipher questions on the Unassisted Leaderboard. Successfully solving these preliminary puzzles may provide valuable insights or clues that could assist you during the main event. The points awarded for the flags will also count towards your total. This is an excellent way to start flexing your investigative muscles early! Don’t worry, if you miss a week’s cipher, as it will stay open through the live event to solve. They’ll be posted on both boards during the main event. Challenge preparation workshop Monday, February 8 at 12:00PM ET Want to sharpen your skills before the competition? Join Kevin Pagano and me for a virtual workshop featuring tips, strategies, and practical advice to help you succeed in the CTF. You can register as part of your Magnet Virtual Summit session selection . Capture the Flag details The challenge itself will be held online on Thursday, February 11, from 11:00 AM – 2:00 PM ET and is open to all registered attendees of Magnet Virtual Summit. To ensure all participants have adequate time for initial preparation, the forensic images will be distributed to all registrants by February 9. This allows for downloading, initial processing, and evidence review prior to the start of the competition. This event is open to participants worldwide. Ready to compete? Register for the Magnet Virtual Summit 2027 CTF here . We strongly encourage you to register without delay, as the evidence images will be distributed in advance to facilitate preparation. Additionally, make sure to follow our updates on LinkedIn , where we will share posts that may contain helpful hints or important references. Please make sure to register with Magnet Forensics by February 8, at 4:00 PM ET as well as the CTF board itself with the same email address. We are truly looking forward to your participation in the Magnet Virtual Summit CTF. Best of luck to all competitors!

items.title: AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors and Use AV Drivers to Kill EDR Process
items.summary: A ransomware group called AuditTeam is dressing up extortion as a paid security audit. Victims get a ransom note that reads like an audit log. It asks for an “Audit & Consulting fee” in return for a report on the holes the attackers used to get in. Before the note appears, the group has already shut down security tools with a signed antivirus driver and encrypted the files. The campaign ran from January 2026 through at least October 2026. It hit dozens of organizations, and a recent report on crews that disable EDR shows why this step matters so much to modern ransomware gangs. Researchers at Securelist, the research arm of Kaspersky, identified the malware and named its framework OpsAgent. They first saw it on March 10, 2026, in an intrusion at a company in Hong Kong. The tool looked like a normal penetration testing kit. Further digging showed the same tool in other countries. The Securelist team says AuditTeam’s victims include organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also lists victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan and Spain. AuditTeam Ransomware Gang Poses as Security Auditors The EDR killer is an add-on module for OpsAgent. It installs a driver that poses as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus, from the KV product series. The driver carries a valid digital signature, which helps it load without raising alarms. This trick is called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, or BYOVD. Attackers bring a trusted, signed driver onto a machine and misuse it to run code at the kernel level, where security tools have little power to fight back. Once the driver is loaded, the malware talks to it through a filter port named \KvCorePortX0. When the driver gets the command 0x1D followed by a file name, it ends the matching process. The kill list holds about 220 names. It covers Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng), ESET (ekrn) and Kaspersky (avp). It also covers monitoring tools such as Sysmon, splunkd and wazuh-agent. Remote access tools like TeamViewer, backup services such as Veeam and Acronis, and database engines such as sqlservr, mysqld, mongod and redis-server are on it too. Other gangs use the same idea. Earlier reporting on how GentleKiller abused vulnerable drivers showed one gang killing more than 400 security processes before it encrypted anything. The ransom note (Source – Securelist) After the security tools go down, the cryptor module takes over. It encrypts files with AES-CBC or ChaCha20 and gives each file its own key. It also uses X25519 key exchange, so victims cannot easily recover the keys. The module stops database and backup services, deletes shadow copies and empties the recycle bin. When it deletes files, it overwrites them with random data first, which makes forensic recovery much harder. The same backup-wrecking habit appears in how DeadLock ransomware targets backups before locking files. The ransom note says nothing about encryption. Because the cryptor module drops it, anyone who sees the note already has encrypted files. OpsAgent Tooling, Infrastructure and Defense OpsAgent does a lot. It manages files and processes, injects shellcode, steals tokens, logs keystrokes, takes screenshots and moves between machines. Securelist says it rivals Cobalt Strike in features. Its loaders push code into msiexec.exe, and the newest Rust loader runs the payload inside its own process instead. During the campaign, the authors rewrote the implant from C++ to Rust. Securelist also saw code patterns that suggest the authors used AI tools to help write it. For command and control, the malware uses Amazon CloudFront subdomains. It finds them by reading a public GitHub repository. Because CloudFront addresses are shared with legitimate traffic, blocking by IP address does not work well. The GitHub repository was removed in November 2026. The latest Rust samples have that feature switched off, so the campaign is probably still running. Defenders should watch for new kernel driver installs, especially a file named kvcore.sys. They should alert on any security agent that stops reporting while its host stays online. Turning on Microsoft’s vulnerable driver blocklist and limiting local admin rights also helps. Even trusted vendor tools can be turned against you, as research on how a Microsoft Defender driver abused can disable endpoint protection shows. Keep offline backups, because this gang destroys the online ones. items.title: Hackers Actively Exploit Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw to Execute Code Without Authentication
items.summary: Hackers are actively exploiting a critical vulnerability in Apache Roller that lets them run code on affected servers without signing in, the Apache Software Foundation warned on November 17. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129448, affects versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 out of 10. Apache says administrators should upgrade to Roller 6.1.6 or later. Version 6.1.5 is also vulnerable, but Apache tracks it under a separate CVE. Apache Roller is a Java-based blogging platform that can host multiple blogs and support teams of writers and editors. The vulnerability is in its XML-RPC endpoint, an interface that lets other software communicate with Roller. The server accepts certain extended data types and rebuilds them into objects before checking whether the sender is allowed to use the service. That process, known as deserialization, is unsafe when the server reconstructs data supplied by an attacker. The result is remote code execution, or RCE . An attacker who can reach the vulnerable service over the network can run code without a valid account or any action from a blog user. items.title: Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software to Execute SYSTEM Commands and Dump Active Directory Data
items.summary: Exploited CyberPower PowerPanel Business software for managing uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) to gain SYSTEM-level access to a Windows domain controller. Symantec reported on November 18 that the attackers used a built-in scripting feature to copy the Active Directory database and launch malware that kept running after the collection activity. Researchers did not observe data leaving the network or see ransomware deployed. PowerPanel Business helps businesses keep servers running during brief power interruptions and shut them down safely during longer outages. Its event settings let administrators run scripts when power drops or fails. On Windows, the PowerPanel service, ppbed.exe, runs as SYSTEM, a built-in account with extensive local privileges. Scripts started by the service inherit those permissions. In the incident, Symantec traced unauthorized scripts to the PowerPanel web console on TCP port 3052. The service launched Windows Command Prompt, and the resulting activity included downloading tools and running a PowerShell test that loaded a small .NET program into memory. The program only printed a greeting, but it showed that the attackers could run code in memory through a trusted service. Symantec did not establish how the attackers first gained console access. Earlier advisories documented hard-coded credentials, a default administrator password and a file-upload flaw in PowerPanel Business. Hackers Abuse CyberPower UPS Software Stolen administrator credentials were another possibility. Cyber Security News previously covered security flaws in PowerPanel Enterprise , a separate CyberPower product. Those findings do not establish how this intrusion began. The attackers repeatedly changed their collection scripts and checked the results before trying again. They eventually copied ntds. dit, the Active Directory database, and collected the SYSTEM registry hive. Attack chain (source: Symantec ) As our earlier coverage of Active Directory database theft explains, access to both files can expose password hashes and other secrets used to authenticate domain accounts. Symantec said the repeated adjustments suggested someone was operating the tools live. It did not name a threat group or determine the attacker’s motive. The same PowerPanel process tree later led to upnpcont.exe, an executable named after a Microsoft component. It ran from an unusual location under the SYSTEM profile and loaded a malicious atl.dll. The technique, known as DLL side-loading , uses a legitimate program to load a malicious code library. The link back to ppbed.exe gave defenders a way to connect the malware with the earlier activity. Symantec recommends finding every PowerPanel Business installation and limiting access to TCP port 3052 to approved administrator workstations. Keep the console off the public internet and away from regular user networks. Apply vendor updates, replace default passwords with unique credentials, and review the settings that link power events to scripts. Check the extcmd and temp\profile\extcmd folders for scripts that do not match a known configuration. On domain controllers, review endpoint logs for unusual command shells, PowerShell activity, or database access linked to ppbed.exe. Use Symantec’s incident report to compare file names and hashes with evidence from affected hosts. If the evidence shows that the directory database was copied, treat domain credentials as potentially exposed even without proof of an outbound transfer. Plan a coordinated reset of krbtgt, the account used to sign Kerberos authentication tickets, alongside wider credential rotation. items.title: Hackers Exploiting Java4Shell RCE Flaw Using ARTEX Disguise Themselves as Chrome
items.summary: Cloudflare’s Cloudforce One reported a Java4Shell exploit attempt that looked like ordinary Google Chrome traffic in web logs. The team said a source IP first scanned a target using a User-Agent header that gave away the scanning tool. About 17 hours later, the same address sent an exploit attempt to the same target, this time claiming to be Chrome. In a separate November 18 update, Cloudforce One said it had seen traffic linked to both ARTEX and Java4Shell from a single IP address for the first time. The two updates do not establish that ARTEX sent the Chrome-disguised request or that either attempt led to a breach. The disguise was in the HTTP User-Agent header, which identifies the client making a web request, not in Chrome itself. Today, Nov 18, at 06:59:34 we saw the first instance of ARTEX and Java4Shell being used from the same IP address. This indicates threat actors are combining new vulnerabilities to carry out attacks. — Cloudforce One (@Cloudforce_One) November 18, 2026 Java4Shell Puts Java Servers at Risk Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, affects the Base64 decoder in OpenJDK’s HotSpot runtime. Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. On affected systems, the decoder can write outside its assigned memory when it processes invalid input. The flaw can crash a Java service, expose data held in memory, or allow remote code execution (RCE), meaning an attacker can run code on the target. As Cyber Security News reported in its Java4Shell coverage , the flaw is in the Java runtime itself, not a library such as Log4j. It requires an unpatched Java build, an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support, and an application that passes attacker-controlled data to the affected decoder. ARM64 systems do not use that vulnerable code path. Calif’s research demonstrated code execution without a login in default test setups of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, and PingFederate. Those tests show what is possible under the right conditions. They do not show that the target in Cloudforce One’s report was running any of those products or that the request succeeded. The FBI’s November 13 advisory describes ARTEX as an AI-driven security testing framework that attackers have used to speed up intrusions. It cites separate campaigns involving South Korean financial institutions and ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers. Cyber Security News has also covered ARTEX consoles exposed to the internet . Neither report ties those earlier findings to the Java4Shell request that posed as Chrome. Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17. Fixed OpenJDK builds include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1. Administrators should check their Java vendor’s advisory and prioritize internet-facing services. After restarting a service, verify the Java version it actually loads, not just the version returned by the host’s default Java command. For incident review, compare web and application logs for repeat requests to the same service, then check host logs for unexpected Java crashes or unusual activity. A Chrome label is not proof that a real browser sent the request, and a shared IP is not proof of a common operator. The FBI advises checking IP indicators against current network activity before using them to block traffic. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: WordPress 7.1.5 Patches 20 Security Issues, Including Potential RCE and SQL Injection Flaws
items.summary: WordPress released version 7.1.5 on November 18, 2026, to address 20 security issues in WordPress Core. The update fixes a flaw that could allow someone without an account to run code on a vulnerable server, two SQL injection flaws, and a weakness that could let an administrator of one site take over a WordPress Multisite network. WordPress recommends updating immediately. Security researcher Logan Homolka reported the flaw in the Template Part block, which WordPress uses for shared layout elements such as headers and footers. The flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker gain permissions they should not have and could lead to remote code execution (RCE). The announcement does not report attacks exploiting it or identify which site configurations could allow code execution. The Template Part flaw is separate from the update-process weakness covered in our WordPress 7.1.4 security release report . The new release also fixes a distinct Multisite issue, reported by Yuval Miller, that could let a site Administrator take over a Super Admin account. That distinction matters because a Super Admin can manage the entire network, not just one site. SQL Injection, XSS, and Data Exposure Christiaan Swiers reported SQL injection in WP_Meta_Query , which builds database queries based on metadata. WordPress security team member Rudy Faile reported the second flaw, which affects front-page previews in the Customizer. SQL injection can change how a database interprets a query. The two flaws are separate from the export-related issue fixed in WordPress 7.1.3 . Several fixes address cross-site scripting (XSS), which can let an attacker run a script in another user’s browser. One stored XSS flaw affects comments and does not require an account. Other fixes cover the legacy media library, embeds, and the block editor. The update also closes a data leak that exposed private taxonomy terms, such as categories or tags, through REST API search without a login. The official WordPress release announcement also lists a denial-of-service flaw involving XML-RPC pingbacks and a permissions bypass in comment editing. The 20 entries include two preventive changes: stricter checks for JSON content types and removal of an Imgur embed option whose provider was already gone. How to Update WordPress Open Dashboard → Updates → Update Now, then confirm the installed version. Sites with automatic background updates can receive the patch without manual action, but administrators should still verify that it installed. For older deployments, the WordPress 7.1.5 documentation lists patched versions by branch, including 7.0.9, 6.9.12, and 4.7.40. WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates. Patches for older branches give administrators a way to close these flaws if they cannot move to 7.1.5 right away, but WordPress says only the latest version is actively supported. WordPress 7.2 Release Candidate 2 also contains the applicable fixes. The final 7.2 release is planned for December 8, but site owners should install the available security update now rather than wait. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? items.title: PHP Security Team Warns of Critical Vulnerabilities, Urges Users to Prepare for November 19 Updates
items.summary: The PHP security team plans to release security updates on Thursday, November 19, 2026, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC. In its November 18 security notice , the team said the releases will address vulnerabilities across all supported PHP branches, with the highest severity rated critical. It urged users to prepare now and install the updates promptly once they are available. The patches are part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle. The team said the critical issues require non-default settings or uncommon setups. An application might run a vulnerable PHP version without meeting the requirements for an attack. The team will release technical details and the corresponding fixed version numbers along with the updates. PHP Session Upload Progress Flaw One expected fix addresses CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw tied to PHP’s session upload progress feature. The feature lets an application track a file upload while it is still in progress. Under certain conditions, the flaw could let an attacker run code on the server. PHP first flagged the issue on October 23, saying it requires an unusual combination of settings and application code. For deployments covered by the advisory, PHP recommends disabling session upload progress as a temporary safeguard. Teams that have already turned it off should keep it disabled until they install the fix. PHP says applications that do not change how session data is stored while running can leave the feature enabled. The patch window also falls on the planned launch date for PHP 8.6.0. Administrators do not need to move to the new feature release just to get the security fixes. The team plans to publish updates for existing supported branches. October’s PHP2Shell Attacks The November update follows October’s emergency PHP2Shell patches . That release fixed CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. Both flaws scored 9.2 out of 10 and could let attackers run code on affected web servers without logging in. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of CISA’s PHP2Shell warning , the agency added both October flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after attacks were reported. That warning applies to the October flaws and does not establish that attackers are exploiting the issues covered by the November release. Check which PHP versions actually serve web requests, including those bundled in containers or managed by hosting providers. Once the updates go live, consult the PHP 2026 release archive for the fixed version on your branch. Install that build or your vendor’s patched package, restart the affected PHP workers, and verify that the web application is running the updated version. Checking only the command-line version may miss an older build still serving traffic. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #493: Why your AI model could be a sleeper agent
items.summary: You join a video call, and your contact and a few colleagues are already there, waiting patiently. But they can't hear you, and a pop-up says you need to install an update to fix your microphone. What could possibly go wrong? Meanwhile, we explain how changing just a handful of numbers can turn an AI model into a sleeper agent, waiting for the right moment to strike. Plus, Andrius Buinovskis of NordLayer explains how companies can see which AI tools their staff are really using, and stop sensitive data leaking out, without banning AI altogether. All this and more in episode 493 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Ray Redacted.

items.title: Age of Entitlement: Privileges in Entra's access packages
items.summary: This series will describe how everyday access package configurations within entitlement management can lead to scenarios where an attacker could elevate privileges. This post lays out the fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID Governance's entitlement management, and why an attacker may target for privilege escalation.

items.title: How Datadog resolves evolving OpenTelemetry semantics at query time
items.summary: OpenTelemetry conventions evolve, but queries still need to work across old, current, and Datadog-native telemetry. Learn how Datadog uses a knowledge graph and query-time translation to resolve conditional semantic equivalences and validate them against real data.

items.title: Drone Hacking Part 2: Authorized ~_~ by Potensic ~_~
items.summary: With the Potensic Atom 2's firmware in hand, we trade soldering irons for disassemblers and reverse engineer the drone, its remote, and the companion app. Along the way, we explore its custom protocol, the firmware encryption, a predictable WiFi password, and two undocumented "debug features" that get us a root shell on the drone.
items.summary_html:
With the Potensic Atom 2's firmware in hand, we trade soldering irons for disassemblers and reverse engineer the drone, its remote, and the companion app.
Along the way, we explore its custom protocol, the firmware encryption, a predictable WiFi password, and two undocumented "debug features" that get us a root shell on the drone.
